title: The epipelagic zone
text: The epipelagic or sunlight zone is the uppermost layer of the open ocean, from the surface to about 200 metres. Enough sunlight reaches it for photosynthesis, so it holds nearly all the ocean's plant-like plankton and most familiar marine life, from tuna to dolphins.

title: The mesopelagic twilight zone
text: The mesopelagic or twilight zone lies roughly between 200 and 1,000 metres deep. Sunlight fades to near darkness and photosynthesis cannot occur, yet faint light lingers. Many of its animals glow with their own light, and vast numbers rise at night to feed near the surface.

title: The bathypelagic midnight zone
text: The bathypelagic or midnight zone spans roughly 1,000 to 4,000 metres, where no sunlight reaches and the water is cold and dark. Animals here rely on food sinking from above or on their own light, and pressures reach hundreds of times that at the surface.

title: The abyssopelagic zone
text: The abyssopelagic zone lies between about 4,000 and 6,000 metres deep, covering much of the deep ocean floor. Temperatures hover just above freezing, food is scarce, and its creatures are adapted to crushing pressure and everlasting darkness.

title: The hadal zone
text: The hadal zone, named for the Greek underworld, comprises the deepest waters below about 6,000 metres, found mainly in trenches. Despite extreme pressure and cold, it supports specialised life such as amphipods, sea cucumbers, and certain fishes of the depths.

title: Pelagic and benthic realms
text: Oceanographers distinguish the pelagic realm, the open water column, from the benthic realm, the sea floor and the life upon it. Pelagic animals swim or drift freely, while benthic creatures such as crabs, corals, and clams are tied to the bottom.

title: The photic and aphotic zones
text: The photic zone is the sunlit surface layer where enough light penetrates for photosynthesis, usually the upper 200 metres. Below lies the aphotic zone, where light is too weak to sustain plants, and life depends on food drifting down from above.

title: The neritic zone
text: The neritic zone is the relatively shallow water overlying the continental shelf, from the low-tide line out to roughly 200 metres. Well lit and rich in nutrients from the land, it is among the most biologically productive parts of the whole ocean.

title: The intertidal zone
text: The intertidal or littoral zone is the shore between the highest and lowest tide marks, alternately submerged and exposed. Its inhabitants, such as barnacles, mussels, and limpets, must endure waves, changing temperature, and spells of drying air.

title: The oceanic zone
text: The oceanic zone is the vast open sea beyond the continental shelf, where the water is deep and generally poorer in nutrients than coastal waters. It is divided by depth and light into the sunlit, twilight, midnight, and deeper layers.

title: Ocean surface currents
text: Surface currents are large, persistent flows of water driven mainly by prevailing winds, guided by the Earth's rotation and the shape of the continents. They spread heat around the globe, moderating climate and carrying nutrients and organisms far and wide.

title: The Gulf Stream
text: The Gulf Stream is a powerful warm current flowing from the Gulf of Mexico up the eastern coast of North America and across the Atlantic toward Europe. It carries enormous heat, contributing to the mild climate of northwestern Europe.

title: Ocean gyres
text: A gyre is a large system of circular currents formed by wind patterns and the Earth's rotation. Five major subtropical gyres turn in the North and South Atlantic, the North and South Pacific, and the Indian Ocean, each wheeling slowly around its basin.

title: The Coriolis effect
text: The Coriolis effect is the apparent deflection of moving air and water caused by the Earth's rotation. In the Northern Hemisphere it curves currents to the right, and in the Southern to the left, shaping the circular flow of the great ocean gyres.

title: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current
text: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows clockwise around Antarctica, unbroken by any land. It is the largest current by volume, linking the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans and helping to isolate Antarctica within a cold, encircling flow of water.

title: The Kuroshio Current
text: The Kuroshio, or Japan Current, is a warm, swift current flowing northeastward past eastern Japan in the North Pacific. Like the Atlantic's Gulf Stream, it carries tropical heat poleward and strongly shapes the region's climate and fisheries.

title: The California Current
text: The California Current is a cold current flowing southward along the western coast of North America. It brings cool, nutrient-rich water and promotes coastal upwelling, feeding productive fisheries and helping to raise the region's summer fog.

title: The Humboldt Current
text: The Humboldt or Peru Current is a cold current flowing north along the western coast of South America. Its intense upwelling of nutrient-rich water makes it one of the most productive marine regions on Earth, teeming with fish and seabirds.

title: The Agulhas Current
text: The Agulhas Current is a warm, fast current flowing southward along the southeastern coast of Africa. Where it meets the cold Atlantic near the Cape, it can shed large eddies that carry warm Indian Ocean water into the Atlantic.

title: Deep ocean currents
text: Beneath the wind-driven surface flows, slow but massive deep currents move through the ocean, driven by differences in water density rather than wind. They carry cold, dense water from the polar regions along the sea floor toward the equator.

title: Boundary currents
text: Ocean gyres have fast, narrow currents along the western edges of basins, called western boundary currents, and slower, broader flows along the eastern edges. The Gulf Stream and Kuroshio are classic examples of swift western boundary currents.

title: The North Atlantic Drift
text: The North Atlantic Drift is the continuation of the Gulf Stream that carries warm water northeast across the ocean toward Europe. Its gentle warmth keeps harbours ice-free far north and softens the winters of the lands along its path.

title: The Canary Current
text: The Canary Current is a cool current flowing south along the coast of northwestern Africa. It forms part of the North Atlantic gyre and, with the upwelling it brings, supports a rich fishery along that stretch of the African shore.

title: The cause of tides
text: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, caused chiefly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser degree, the Sun on the Earth's oceans. As the Earth turns beneath these raised bulges of water, coasts pass through high and low tides.

title: Spring and neap tides
text: Spring tides are especially high and low tides near the new and full Moon, when the Sun and Moon pull in line and reinforce each other. Neap tides, with smaller range, occur near the quarter Moons, when Sun and Moon pull at right angles.

title: Semidiurnal and diurnal tides
text: Many coasts have two high and two low tides each day, called a semidiurnal pattern. Others have only one of each, a diurnal pattern, while some have mixed tides with unequal highs and lows, according to the shape of the coast and sea floor.

title: Tidal range
text: Tidal range is the vertical difference between high and low water. It varies greatly, from a few centimetres in some enclosed seas to more than fifteen metres where a basin's natural rhythm resonates with the tide, as in the Bay of Fundy.

title: The Bay of Fundy tides
text: The Bay of Fundy in eastern Canada has the greatest tidal range on Earth, exceeding sixteen metres in places. Its funnel shape and a resonance with the tidal period cause the incoming water to pile up to extraordinary heights twice each day.

title: Tidal currents
text: As tides rise and fall, they drive horizontal movements of water called tidal currents. The incoming flood current and outgoing ebb current can run swiftly through narrow channels, and near slack water the flow briefly pauses before reversing.

title: The Moon and tidal timing
text: Because the Moon orbits in the same direction the Earth spins, the tidal cycle runs a little longer than a solar day. High tides therefore arrive roughly fifty minutes later each day, tracking the Moon's slow progress across the sky.

title: Tidal bore
text: A tidal bore is a wall of water that rushes up certain rivers as the rising tide meets the outflowing stream. Where the river narrows and shallows sharply, the incoming tide is forced into a single surging wave that travels far upstream.

title: How ocean waves form
text: Most ocean waves are made by wind blowing across the water, transferring its energy to the sea. The stronger the wind, the longer it blows, and the greater the open distance over which it acts, the larger the resulting waves grow.

title: Wave motion versus water motion
text: In a passing wave the energy travels forward, not the water itself. Individual water particles move in small circles, returning nearly to where they began, which is why a floating object bobs up and down rather than being carried along with the wave.

title: Wave crest and trough
text: A wave's highest point is its crest and its lowest its trough. The vertical distance between them is the wave height, the horizontal distance between successive crests is the wavelength, and the time between them is the wave's period.

title: Why waves break
text: As a wave nears shallow water, friction with the bottom slows its base while the top races on. The crest steepens, topples forward, and breaks, releasing its gathered energy as the tumbling white water of surf along the shore.

title: Swell at sea
text: Swell consists of smooth, regular waves that have travelled far from the wind that made them. Having outrun the storm, the waves sort themselves by length and can cross whole oceans to arrive, orderly and long, at distant and calmer shores.

title: Tsunami waves
text: A tsunami is a series of very long waves usually set off by an undersea earthquake, landslide, or eruption that suddenly displaces water. In the open ocean the waves are low but swift, rising to great heights only as they reach shallow coasts.

title: Rogue waves
text: Rogue waves are unusually large, steep waves that appear without warning, far higher than the surrounding sea. They can arise when separate wave trains combine or when waves meet an opposing current, and they pose a grave danger to ships.

title: Fetch and wave size
text: Fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows to raise waves. A longer fetch, with stronger and more sustained wind, builds larger waves, which is why the greatest seas develop over the vast reaches of the open ocean.

title: Wave energy
text: The energy in a wave grows sharply with its height, so a wave twice as tall carries several times the force. This is why storm waves batter coasts and vessels with such power, and why even distant storms can send heavy surf to quiet shores.

title: Standing waves
text: A standing wave forms when waves reflect and combine so that certain points rise and fall while others stay still. In enclosed bays and harbours such oscillations, called seiches, can slosh the water back and forth like tea in a rocked cup.

title: Ocean salinity
text: Salinity is the measure of dissolved salts in seawater, averaging about thirty-five grams per kilogram of water, or roughly three and a half percent. Sodium and chloride, the makings of common table salt, form most of this dissolved matter.

title: Sources of ocean salt
text: The salt of the sea comes largely from rivers, which dissolve minerals from rocks on land and carry them to the ocean over immense spans of time. Undersea volcanic vents and the slow weathering of the sea floor also add dissolved salts.

title: The thermocline
text: The thermocline is a layer where temperature drops rapidly with depth, dividing the warm, sunlit surface waters from the cold, dark deep water below. It acts as a barrier that limits the mixing of the two, keeping the depths perpetually cold.

title: The halocline
text: The halocline is a zone where salinity changes sharply with depth. It often forms where fresh water from rivers or melting ice floats atop denser, saltier water beneath, creating a stable boundary between layers of differing saltiness.

title: The pycnocline
text: The pycnocline is the layer where water density rises rapidly with depth, driven by changes in temperature, salinity, or both. This dense boundary resists vertical mixing and helps keep surface and deep waters largely apart.

title: The mixed surface layer
text: The upper ocean is stirred by wind and waves into a mixed layer of nearly uniform temperature, often tens of metres deep. Below it the temperature falls away through the thermocline into the cold, still water of the deep sea.

title: Why the deep ocean is cold
text: Nearly all the deep ocean is cold, only a few degrees above freezing, because its water sinks from the polar seas where the surface is chilled. Sunlight warms only the thin surface layer, leaving the vast depths in permanent cold.

title: The colour of the ocean
text: The ocean appears blue because water absorbs the longer red and yellow rays of sunlight more than the shorter blue ones, which are scattered back to our eyes. Coastal waters may look green or brown where sediment and plankton abound.

title: Brackish water
text: Brackish water is a mixture of fresh and salt water, saltier than a river but less salty than the sea. It gathers in estuaries and coastal marshes where rivers meet the ocean, and it shelters creatures suited to its shifting saltiness.

title: Thermohaline circulation
text: Thermohaline circulation is the global movement of ocean water driven by differences in temperature and salinity, which together set its density. Cold, salty water sinks in the polar seas and creeps along the deep before rising elsewhere, in a slow worldwide loop.

title: The global conveyor belt
text: The great ocean conveyor is the linked system of surface and deep currents that carries water slowly around the world over centuries. It transports heat, salt, and dissolved gases between ocean basins and helps regulate the climate of the Earth.

title: Deep water formation
text: In the cold seas near Greenland and Antarctica, surface water grows so cold and salty that it becomes dense enough to sink. This sinking, called deep water formation, drives the deep branch of the circulation that feeds the world's oceans.

title: Coastal upwelling
text: Upwelling occurs where winds push surface water away from a coast, allowing cold, nutrient-rich water to rise from below in its place. This nourishes plankton and feeds some of the richest fisheries in the world along certain coastlines.

title: Equatorial upwelling
text: Along the equator, winds and the Earth's rotation draw surface waters apart, drawing deeper water upward to replace them. This equatorial upwelling brings nutrients toward the surface and enriches the life of a band across the tropical oceans.

title: El Nino
text: El Nino is a periodic warming of the surface waters of the tropical eastern Pacific that upsets the usual pattern of winds and currents. It weakens the upwelling off South America, disturbs fisheries, and alters weather across much of the world.

title: La Nina
text: La Nina is the counterpart to El Nino, marked by unusually cool surface waters in the tropical eastern Pacific and strengthened trade winds. Like its warm sibling, it shifts patterns of rain and temperature across many parts of the globe.

title: The water molecule
text: A water molecule is made of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, giving the formula H2O. Its bent shape leaves one side slightly positive and the other slightly negative, making water a polar molecule with remarkable properties.

title: Hydrogen bonding in water
text: Water molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonds, weak links between the slightly positive hydrogen of one and the slightly negative oxygen of another. These bonds give water its high boiling point, surface tension, and many life-giving qualities.

title: Archimedes' principle
text: Archimedes' principle states that an object immersed in a fluid is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. If that buoyant force matches the object's weight, it floats; if the object weighs more, it sinks.

title: Why ships float
text: A ship floats because its hull, though built of heavy steel, encloses a large volume that pushes aside a great weight of water. As long as the weight of water displaced equals the ship's own weight, the upward buoyant force holds the vessel up.

title: Density of water
text: Density is mass per unit of volume, and fresh water is close to one gram per cubic centimetre. Objects less dense than water float and those denser sink, so density decides which materials rise and which fall in the sea.

title: Water pressure with depth
text: Pressure in water rises with depth because of the growing weight of water above. Roughly every ten metres of descent adds one atmosphere of pressure, so deep-sea creatures and vessels endure forces many times greater than those at the surface.

title: Seawater is denser
text: Seawater is denser than fresh water because of its dissolved salt. This is why objects float more readily in the sea than in a lake, and why very salty waters such as the Dead Sea let bathers float with remarkable ease.

title: Surface tension
text: Surface tension is the tendency of a liquid's surface to behave like a stretched skin, arising from the mutual attraction of its molecules. It lets small insects walk on ponds and allows water to gather into rounded droplets.

title: Water's three states
text: Water exists as solid ice, liquid water, and gaseous vapour, and it shifts between these states as temperature and pressure change. This ready change of state drives the water cycle and lies at the heart of weather and climate.

title: Ice floats
text: Unlike most substances, water expands as it freezes, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats. This unusual property lets ice form a protective lid on ponds and seas, allowing life to carry on in the water below.

title: Water's high heat capacity
text: Water can absorb much heat while warming only a little, a property called high specific heat capacity. This lets the oceans store vast amounts of the Sun's energy and so moderate the temperature of the whole planet.

title: Latent heat of water
text: Changing water's state takes energy without changing its temperature, called latent heat. Melting ice absorbs heat and evaporating water absorbs still more, which is why sweat cools the skin and evaporation cools the surface of the sea.

title: Water as a solvent
text: Water is often called the universal solvent, for its polar molecules dissolve a great range of substances, from salts to sugars. This makes seawater a rich chemical broth and makes water essential to the chemistry of every living thing.

title: Capillary action
text: Capillary action is the rise of water in narrow spaces against gravity, caused by its attraction to the surrounding surface together with its own cohesion. It draws water up through soil, paper, and the fine vessels of plants.

title: Displacement of water
text: When an object is placed in water, it pushes aside a volume equal to the part of itself that is submerged. Measuring this displaced volume, as Archimedes is said to have discovered, reveals the object's size and helps explain how it floats.

title: Freezing and boiling points
text: Pure water freezes into ice at zero degrees and boils into vapour at one hundred degrees on the common scale, at ordinary pressure. Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point, which is why the sea can stay liquid below the freezing point of fresh water.

title: Cohesion and adhesion
text: Cohesion is the attraction of water molecules to one another, while adhesion is their attraction to other surfaces. Together they let water cling in drops, creep up narrow tubes, and rise through the tissues of living plants against gravity.

title: How submarines dive
text: A submarine dives by filling its ballast tanks with seawater, making the vessel heavier and less buoyant so that it sinks. To surface, compressed air blows the water out of the tanks, restoring buoyancy and lifting the submarine back toward the top.

title: Ballast tanks
text: Ballast tanks are compartments in a submarine that can be filled with water or air to control the vessel's buoyancy. By adjusting how much water they hold, the crew makes the submarine sink, rise, or hang steady at a chosen depth.

title: Neutral buoyancy
text: A submarine reaches neutral buoyancy when its weight exactly matches the buoyant force of the water it displaces, letting it hang at a set depth without rising or sinking. Careful trimming of the ballast keeps the vessel poised in the water.

title: Ship displacement
text: A ship's displacement is the weight of water it pushes aside, which equals the ship's own weight when it floats. Naval architects measure large vessels by their displacement, since it reflects directly the mass the hull must bear up.

title: Hull design
text: A ship's hull is shaped to move smoothly through the water while giving buoyancy and stability. A streamlined form lessens drag, a deep keel resists sideways drift and helps prevent capsizing, and a broad beam adds steadiness in a rough sea.

title: The keel
text: The keel is the central structural backbone running along the bottom of a ship from bow to stern. It strengthens the hull and, by reaching downward, helps keep the vessel upright and resists the sideways push of wind and current.

title: Propeller propulsion
text: Most modern ships are driven by propellers, rotating blades that push water backward and thrust the vessel forward by reaction. The angled blades act like screws biting into the water, turning the engine's spin into forward motion.

title: The Plimsoll line
text: The Plimsoll line, or load line, is a mark on a ship's hull showing the deepest it may be safely loaded. Because water density varies with temperature and salinity, several marks give safe limits for different waters and seasons.

title: Sonar at sea
text: Sonar, meaning sound navigation and ranging, finds underwater objects by sending out sound pulses and listening for their echoes. Because sound travels well through water, sonar can gauge depth, locate vessels, and map the sea floor.

title: Active and passive sonar
text: Active sonar sends out a sound pulse and times the returning echo to locate objects, while passive sonar simply listens for the sounds vessels and animals make. Submarines often prefer to listen, so as not to betray their own position.

title: The periscope
text: A periscope lets a submerged submarine see above the surface through a vertical tube fitted with mirrors or prisms at each end. Light entering the top is reflected down to the viewer's eye, allowing a look around without exposing the vessel.

title: Why steel ships float
text: Though steel is far denser than water, a steel ship floats because its hull encloses a large hollow space of air. Counting that internal space, the average density of the whole vessel is less than that of water, so it stays afloat.

title: The bow and stern
text: The bow is the forward part of a ship, shaped to cut cleanly through the water, while the stern is the rear, where the rudder and propeller are usually set. A well-formed bow reduces resistance and helps the vessel ride the waves.

title: The rudder
text: A rudder is a flat, movable blade at the stern used for steering. Turning it deflects the flow of water past the hull, which pushes the stern sideways and swings the vessel onto a new heading, letting the helmsman guide the ship.

title: Trim and stability
text: A ship's trim is its balance from bow to stern, and its stability is its tendency to right itself after tilting. Proper loading keeps the centre of gravity low, so that buoyancy swings the vessel upright rather than letting it capsize.

title: Draft of a ship
text: A ship's draft is the vertical distance from the waterline to the bottom of the keel, showing how deep the hull sits in the water. Knowing the draft tells sailors the least depth of water in which the vessel may safely float.

title: Ship anchors
text: An anchor holds a ship in place by digging into the sea floor and resisting the pull of wind and current. Its holding power comes not only from its own weight but from the length of chain lying along the bottom, called the scope.

title: The sail and the wind
text: A sail catches the wind to drive a ship forward, and by trimming it a crew can sail not only before the wind but also at an angle across it. Skilled handling let sailing vessels work their way even toward the quarter from which the wind blew.

title: Tacking against the wind
text: A sailing ship cannot sail straight into the wind, but by tacking, it zigzags forward in a series of angled legs. Turning the bow through the wind at the end of each leg, it makes progress toward a point directly upwind.

title: The bilge and pumps
text: The bilge is the lowest inner part of a ship's hull, where water that leaks or washes aboard collects. Pumps draw this water out to keep the vessel dry and afloat, and keeping the bilge clear has always been a constant duty at sea.

title: The compass binnacle
text: The binnacle is the stand that houses a ship's compass, set before the helmsman where he can steer by it. Fitted with a lamp for night and often with correcting magnets, it holds the compass steady and readable through the ship's motion.

title: The ship's wake
text: A ship's wake is the trail of disturbed and foaming water left behind as it moves. Shaped by the hull's passage, the wake spreads in a V behind the vessel, and its form and length reveal much about the ship's speed and course.

title: The propeller and cavitation
text: When a propeller turns very fast, the pressure behind its blades can drop so low that the water briefly boils into bubbles, a process called cavitation. The collapsing bubbles waste power, wear the blades, and make a tell-tale noise.

title: Latitude on Earth
text: Latitude measures how far north or south a place lies from the equator, given in degrees. The equator is zero degrees, the North Pole ninety degrees north, and the South Pole ninety degrees south, forming lines that circle the globe.

title: Longitude on Earth
text: Longitude measures how far east or west a place lies from a chosen reference line, the prime meridian through Greenwich. Lines of longitude run from pole to pole, and together with latitude they fix any position on the Earth's surface.

title: The prime meridian
text: The prime meridian is the line of zero longitude, by agreement passing through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in England. From it, longitude is counted east and west up to one hundred and eighty degrees, where the halves meet at the date line.

title: The magnetic compass
text: A magnetic compass has a needle that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, pointing roughly toward the north magnetic pole. For centuries it has let sailors hold a course even when the Sun and stars are hidden by cloud.

title: Magnetic declination
text: Magnetic declination is the angle between true north, toward the geographic pole, and magnetic north, where a compass points. Because the two differ from place to place, a navigator must correct the compass reading to steer a true course.

title: Celestial navigation
text: Celestial navigation fixes a ship's position by measuring the angles of the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars above the horizon. With a sextant, an accurate clock, and printed tables, a navigator can find a position far out of sight of land.

title: The sextant
text: A sextant measures the angle between a heavenly body and the horizon by means of mirrors and a graduated arc. Read at a known time, this angle lets a navigator work out latitude and, with an accurate clock, longitude as well.

title: Finding latitude by the stars
text: Latitude can be found in the Northern Hemisphere by measuring how high Polaris, the North Star, stands above the horizon, since its angle nearly equals one's latitude. The height of the noon Sun serves the same purpose anywhere on Earth.

title: The marine chronometer
text: The marine chronometer is an exceptionally accurate clock that keeps the time of a reference meridian at sea. By comparing local time from the Sun with the chronometer, navigators at last solved the old problem of finding longitude.

title: Nautical charts
text: A nautical chart is a map of the sea and coast showing depths, hazards, currents, and aids to navigation. Mariners plot their course upon it, choosing safe passages and shunning shoals, rocks, and other dangers to the ship.

title: The knot as a speed
text: A knot is a unit of speed equal to one nautical mile an hour. Its name recalls an old way of measuring speed by counting the knots tied at intervals in a line paid out behind a ship over a timed interval.

title: The nautical mile
text: A nautical mile is a unit of distance at sea equal to about one minute of latitude along a meridian, roughly 1,852 metres. By tying distance to the geometry of the globe, it is well suited to the reckonings of navigation.

title: Coastal lighthouses
text: A lighthouse is a tower bearing a bright light that warns ships of dangerous coasts, rocks, or shoals and guides them safely toward harbour. Each shows a distinct pattern of flashes so that sailors may know it and fix their position.

title: Buoys and beacons
text: Buoys and beacons are floating or fixed markers that guide vessels through safe channels and warn of hazards. Their colours, shapes, and lights follow agreed systems, so that mariners may read the way ahead at a single glance.

title: Dead reckoning
text: Dead reckoning estimates a ship's present position from a known starting point, using its recorded heading, speed, and the time elapsed. Though wind and current introduce error, it remains a valuable check upon other means of navigation.

title: The compass rose
text: The compass rose is the ringed figure on a chart or compass showing directions. It is divided into the cardinal points north, east, south, and west, and further into the thirty-two traditional points that sailors once knew by name.

title: The lead line
text: Before electronic sounders, sailors measured depth by lowering a lead weight on a marked line, a practice called sounding. Tallow set in the weight's base could even bring up a sample of the bottom to help fix the ship's position.

title: Great circle routes
text: The shortest path between two points on the globe follows a great circle, a line whose plane passes through the centre of the Earth. Long-distance ships steer along such routes to save distance, though they appear curved upon a flat chart.

title: The log and speed
text: A ship's speed was long measured with a log, a weighted board streamed astern on a knotted line. By counting how many knots ran out in a set time, sailors reckoned the vessel's speed, and from it estimated the distance run.

title: The traverse board
text: The traverse board was a simple wooden aid on which sailors marked, with pegs, the course steered and the speed made good through each half-hour of a watch. It helped them keep a running record for their dead reckoning.

title: Rhumb lines
text: A rhumb line is a course that crosses every meridian at the same angle, so a ship following it holds a steady compass heading. On the common Mercator chart such a course appears as a straight line, though it is not the shortest path.

title: The astrolabe
text: The mariner's astrolabe was an early instrument for measuring the height of the Sun or a star above the horizon. A graduated ring hung so as to stay upright, and by sighting along its movable arm the navigator read off the angle.

title: The Pole Star and true north
text: Polaris stands so near the point above the Earth's northern axis that it scarcely moves through the night while the other stars wheel about it. Sailors long used it to find true north and to reckon their latitude from its height.

title: The Pacific Ocean
text: The Pacific is the largest and deepest of the oceans, covering about a third of the Earth's surface and holding more than half its free water. It reaches from the Arctic to the Southern Ocean and from Asia and Australia to the Americas.

title: The Atlantic Ocean
text: The Atlantic is the second largest ocean, dividing the Americas from Europe and Africa. Down its centre runs the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a great undersea mountain chain, and it slowly widens as new sea floor spreads on either side.

title: The Indian Ocean
text: The Indian Ocean is the third largest, bounded by Africa, Asia, and Australia. Warm through much of its extent, it is strongly ruled by the seasonal monsoon winds, which reverse direction and drive its surface currents through the year.

title: The Arctic Ocean
text: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest, surrounding the North Pole and largely covered by drifting sea ice. Cold and ringed by the northern lands, it joins the Atlantic broadly and, through a narrow strait, the Pacific.

title: The Southern Ocean
text: The Southern Ocean encircles Antarctica, marked by cold waters and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current that flows unbroken around the continent. Its stormy seas and rich waters teem with krill, whales, seals, and seabirds.

title: The Mediterranean Sea
text: The Mediterranean is a nearly enclosed sea between Europe, Africa, and Asia, joined to the Atlantic by the narrow Strait of Gibraltar. Warm, salty, and almost tideless, it has been a cradle of seafaring peoples for thousands of years.

title: The Mariana Trench
text: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific holds the deepest known point of the ocean, the Challenger Deep, reaching nearly eleven kilometres down. There the crushing pressure and endless dark make one of the most extreme places on Earth.

title: Ocean trenches
text: Ocean trenches are long, narrow, very deep gashes in the sea floor, formed where one slab of the Earth's crust plunges beneath another. The deepest places in the sea, they mark the boundaries where crustal plates collide.

title: Mid-ocean ridges
text: Mid-ocean ridges are vast undersea mountain ranges running through the world's oceans where the sea floor is spreading apart. Molten rock rises along them to form new crust, making them the longest mountain chains on the planet.

title: The continental shelf
text: The continental shelf is the gently sloping, submerged edge of a continent, covered by relatively shallow sea. Rich in sunlight and nutrients, its waters are highly productive and support most of the world's fisheries.

title: The continental slope
text: Beyond the continental shelf the sea floor drops away more steeply along the continental slope, descending toward the deep ocean floor. Submarine canyons often cut through it, channelling sediment downward into the depths.

title: The abyssal plain
text: The abyssal plains are the vast, flat expanses of the deep ocean floor, lying several kilometres beneath the surface. Blanketed by fine sediment settled over ages, they are among the flattest and least known regions on Earth.

title: The Strait of Gibraltar
text: The Strait of Gibraltar is the narrow passage joining the Mediterranean to the Atlantic between Spain and Morocco. Only about fourteen kilometres wide at its narrowest, it is a vital gateway for shipping and for marine life alike.

title: The Gulf of Mexico
text: The Gulf of Mexico is a large ocean basin bordered by the United States, Mexico, and Cuba. Its warm waters help feed the Gulf Stream, and its shape and shallows make it prone to powerful hurricanes in the warmer months.

title: The Bering Strait
text: The Bering Strait is the narrow channel between Asia and North America joining the Arctic and Pacific Oceans. Shallow and often icy, it marks the boundary between two continents, and in ages past a land bridge joined its shores.

title: The Sargasso Sea
text: The Sargasso Sea is a region of the North Atlantic bounded not by land but by the currents circling within a gyre. Named for its floating mats of Sargassum weed, it shelters young sea turtles and is the breeding ground of eels.

title: The Red Sea
text: The Red Sea is a long, narrow arm of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Arabia, lying along a rift where the crust is slowly pulling apart. Warm, salty, and fringed with coral reefs, it is slowly widening into a future ocean.

title: The Dead Sea
text: The Dead Sea is a landlocked salt lake between Jordan and Israel, among the saltiest bodies of water on Earth. Its high salinity makes the water so dense that bathers float with ease, and few creatures can live within it.

title: Undersea seamounts
text: Seamounts are underwater mountains, usually of volcanic origin, that rise from the sea floor without reaching the surface. They stir passing currents, drawing nutrients upward, and their slopes often teem with corals, fish, and other life.

title: Coral atolls
text: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef enclosing a lagoon, formed as a reef grows around a volcanic island that later sinks beneath the sea. Charles Darwin first explained their origin through the slow subsidence of the island.

title: The English Channel
text: The English Channel is the narrow arm of the Atlantic dividing southern England from northern France. One of the busiest sea lanes in the world, its swift tides and frequent fogs have long tested the skill of those who sail it.

title: The Caribbean Sea
text: The Caribbean Sea lies between the Americas, ringed by islands and warmed by the tropical Sun. Its clear, warm waters nourish coral reefs, feed the Gulf Stream through the Gulf of Mexico, and were long crossed by ships of trade and war.

title: The North Sea
text: The North Sea is a shallow arm of the Atlantic between Britain, Scandinavia, and the European mainland. Its stormy, tide-swept waters have long supported rich fisheries and a busy traffic of ships among the surrounding lands.

title: The Baltic Sea
text: The Baltic Sea is a nearly enclosed northern sea, so fed by rivers and rain that its water is only faintly salty. Its brackish, chilly waters freeze in the hardest winters and host a mingling of fresh-water and marine life.

title: The Black Sea
text: The Black Sea is a large inland sea connected to the Mediterranean only by narrow straits. Its deeper waters, cut off from fresh oxygen, are still and lifeless, so that much of its life is confined to a thin surface layer.

title: The Coral Sea
text: The Coral Sea lies off the northeastern coast of Australia, warm and studded with reefs. Along its western edge rises the Great Barrier Reef, and its clear tropical waters shelter an abundance of marine life.

title: The Arabian Sea
text: The Arabian Sea is the northwestern part of the Indian Ocean, bordered by Arabia, Persia, and India. Swept by the seasonal monsoon winds, it has been a highway of trade among these lands since ancient times.

title: The Bay of Bengal
text: The Bay of Bengal is the great northeastern arm of the Indian Ocean, bounded by India and the lands to its east. Fed by mighty rivers and ruled by the monsoon, it is prone to fierce tropical cyclones in season.

title: The Gulf Stream and Europe
text: The warm water carried northeast by the Gulf Stream and its extension keeps the climate of northwestern Europe far milder than its latitude would suggest. Harbours stay ice-free where, at the same distance from the pole, others freeze fast.

title: Submarine canyons
text: Submarine canyons are steep-walled valleys carved into the continental slope and shelf, some as grand as any on land. They channel sediment from the coast into the deep sea and often lie off the mouths of great rivers.

title: The land bridge
text: In times of ice, when much water was locked in glaciers, the sea fell and shallow sea floors rose into land. Such land bridges once joined continents now parted by water, letting animals and peoples cross where the sea now flows.

title: Ocean hurricanes
text: A hurricane is a powerful rotating storm born over warm tropical seas, with fierce winds spiralling around a calm central eye. Fed by heat and moisture from the water, it can bring destructive winds, torrential rain, and a surge of sea onto the land.

title: The eye of a hurricane
text: The eye of a hurricane is the calm, clear centre of the storm, where winds are light and the sky may even clear. Around it swirls the eyewall, a ring of towering cloud where the storm's most violent winds and heaviest rain are found.

title: Storm surge
text: Storm surge is the abnormal rise of sea pushed ashore by a hurricane's winds and low pressure. Often the deadliest part of such a storm, it can flood low coasts far inland, above all when it arrives together with a high tide.

title: Weather fronts
text: A weather front is the boundary between two air masses of different temperature and moisture. Along a cold front, advancing cold air lifts warm air sharply into showers, while a warm front brings gentler, longer rain as warm air rides over cold.

title: The water cycle
text: The water cycle is the endless journey of water through the world. The Sun draws vapour from the sea, it rises and cools into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and runs through rivers and the ground back to the ocean once more.

title: How clouds form
text: Clouds form when moist air rises and cools until its vapour condenses into countless tiny droplets or ice crystals around specks of dust. Gathered in their billions, these droplets scatter light and become visible to us as cloud.

title: Sea fog
text: Sea fog forms when warm, moist air drifts over cooler water, chilling until its vapour condenses into a low cloud at the surface. Common where warm and cold currents meet, it can blanket coasts and hide hazards from passing ships.

title: Trade winds
text: The trade winds are steady winds that blow from the subtropics toward the equator, from the northeast in the north and the southeast in the south. For centuries sailing ships relied on their constancy to carry them across the oceans.

title: The doldrums
text: The doldrums, or intertropical convergence zone, is a belt near the equator where the trade winds meet and rising air leaves the surface winds light and fitful. Sailing ships could lie becalmed there for days beneath towering thunderclouds.

title: The monsoon winds
text: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of the winds that brings a marked change between wet and dry seasons, most famously across southern Asia. In summer moist ocean winds blow inland with heavy rain; in winter the flow reverses and dries.

title: Lightning and thunder
text: Lightning is a sudden discharge of electricity within a storm cloud or between cloud and ground, briefly heating the air to a searing temperature. That rapid heating makes the air expand with a violence heard as the crack of thunder.

title: The Beaufort scale
text: The Beaufort scale describes the strength of the wind at sea by its visible effects, from a calm glassy surface through whitecaps and spray to the mountainous seas of a hurricane. It let sailors judge wind force before instruments were common.

title: Cyclones and typhoons
text: The great tropical storms are called hurricanes in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoons in the western Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean. Though the names differ by region, they are one and the same kind of rotating storm.

title: Waterspouts over the sea
text: A waterspout is a rotating column of air and mist over water, akin to a tornado. Some are weak and brief, spun up beneath a growing cloud, while others are true tornadoes that have wandered from the land out onto the sea.

title: Air pressure and weather
text: Differences in the pressure of the air drive the winds and shape the weather. Air flows from regions of high pressure toward low, and a falling barometer, warning of low pressure moving in, has long foretold the approach of a storm.

title: The jet stream
text: The jet stream is a swift river of wind high in the atmosphere, flowing generally from west to east. It steers the great weather systems along their paths and can hurry or delay ships and aircraft that travel beneath it.

title: Sudden sea squalls
text: A squall is a sudden, sharp increase of wind, often with rain and a swift shift in direction, that sweeps over the sea with little warning. Sailors watch the sky and the surface for the dark line of an approaching squall to shorten sail in time.

title: Sea breezes
text: By day the land warms faster than the sea, and the rising warm air draws a cool breeze in from the water. By night the land cools faster, and the flow reverses, sending a gentle land breeze out toward the sea.

title: How hail forms
text: Hail forms in tall storm clouds when droplets are carried up into freezing air, coated with ice, and tossed up and down until heavy enough to fall. Cut open, a large hailstone shows the layers built during its journey within the cloud.

title: Frost and dew
text: On cool, clear nights the ground loses heat and chills the air just above it. Vapour in that air then condenses into dew, and if the surface is cold enough to freeze the moisture, it settles instead as a delicate coating of frost.

title: Pressure on a diver
text: As a diver descends, the surrounding water pressure rises steadily, adding roughly one atmosphere for every ten metres. This mounting pressure squeezes the air spaces of the body and changes how gases dissolve in the blood.

title: Decompression sickness
text: Decompression sickness, known as the bends, arises when a diver rises too fast and dissolved gases, chiefly nitrogen, form bubbles in the blood and tissues. Slow, staged ascents let the gas leave the body harmlessly through the lungs.

title: Nitrogen narcosis
text: At depth, breathing air under high pressure can cause nitrogen narcosis, a dreamy, drunken state that dulls the judgement. Sometimes called rapture of the deep, it worsens the deeper a diver goes and eases on returning toward the surface.

title: Equalising the ears
text: As pressure grows during a dive, it presses inward on the eardrums, causing pain unless the diver equalises. By gently forcing air into the middle ear through the throat, the pressure on both sides of the eardrum is brought into balance.

title: The lungs under pressure
text: Under water, rising pressure compresses the air in a diver's lungs, and ascent lets it expand again. A breath-hold diver's lungs shrink with depth and refill on rising, which is why an ascending diver on air must never hold the breath.

title: Oxygen toxicity
text: Breathing oxygen at high pressure for too long can turn toxic, harming the lungs and the nervous system. This sets a limit on how deep divers may safely go on oxygen-rich mixtures and shapes the making of breathing gases for deep work.

title: The diving reflex
text: The mammalian diving reflex is an automatic response set off when the face meets cold water. The heart slows and blood draws inward toward the vital organs, sparing oxygen and helping the body endure a breath-hold beneath the surface.

title: Why divers rise slowly
text: Divers ascend slowly and pause at set depths so that nitrogen absorbed under pressure may leave the body little by little. To rush to the surface would let the gas bubble from the blood too fast, risking the painful and dangerous bends.

title: Diving bells
text: A diving bell is a chamber, open at the bottom, lowered into the sea to carry workers underwater. The trapped air within lets them breathe and work for a time on the bottom, and it was among the earliest means of staying below the surface.

title: Breathing gas mixtures
text: For deep or long dives, divers may breathe gases other than ordinary air, blending oxygen with nitrogen or with lighter helium. Such mixtures lessen the perils of narcosis and toxicity, letting divers work safely where plain air would fail them.

title: Ferdinand Magellan
text: Ferdinand Magellan led the expedition that first sailed around the world in the early sixteenth century, though he himself died along the way in the Philippines. His surviving crew's return proved that the world's oceans join into one.

title: James Cook
text: Captain James Cook was an eighteenth-century British navigator who charted much of the Pacific with great care, including New Zealand and the eastern coast of Australia. His accurate surveys and concern for his crew's health set new standards.

title: Christopher Columbus
text: Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 seeking a western route to Asia and instead reached the Americas. His voyages opened lasting contact between the Old and New Worlds, reshaping the history of both.

title: The Challenger expedition
text: The voyage of HMS Challenger in the 1870s was the first great scientific survey of the world's oceans. Over several years it measured depths, temperatures, and currents and catalogued thousands of new creatures, founding the science of oceanography.

title: Vasco da Gama
text: Vasco da Gama was the Portuguese navigator who first sailed from Europe around the southern tip of Africa to India at the close of the fifteenth century. His voyage opened a sea road that transformed trade between Europe and Asia.

title: The Trieste dive
text: In 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste carried two men to the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point in the ocean. Their descent showed that even the ocean's greatest depths, under crushing pressure, are not wholly without life.

title: Fridtjof Nansen
text: Fridtjof Nansen was a Norwegian explorer and scientist who let his ship Fram freeze into the Arctic ice to drift with it, testing ideas about polar currents. His careful observations advanced the young science of the oceans.

title: Jacques Cousteau
text: Jacques Cousteau was a French naval officer and explorer who helped invent an early self-contained breathing device that opened the underwater world to divers. Through his films and books he brought the wonders of the sea to a wide public.

title: The Kon-Tiki voyage
text: In 1947 Thor Heyerdahl sailed a balsa-wood raft, the Kon-Tiki, across the Pacific from South America to Polynesia. His crossing showed that ancient peoples might in principle have made such ocean voyages on simple craft.

title: Zheng He
text: Zheng He was a Chinese admiral of the early fifteenth century who led vast fleets across the Indian Ocean as far as Africa. His great treasure ships were among the largest wooden vessels built anywhere in their age.

title: The Age of Discovery
text: The Age of Discovery was the period from the fifteenth to the seventeenth centuries when European sailors explored and charted much of the world's coasts. Advances in ships, navigation, and mapmaking made these long ocean voyages possible.

title: The search for longitude
text: For centuries sailors could find their latitude but not their longitude at sea, and many ships were lost as a result. The problem was solved in the eighteenth century when John Harrison built clocks accurate enough to keep reference time at sea.

title: The Beagle voyage
text: The survey voyage of HMS Beagle in the 1830s carried the young naturalist Charles Darwin around the world. His observations of the lands and creatures he met, from the Galapagos to the coral reefs, later shaped his ideas on the origin of species.

title: The Endurance expedition
text: Early in the twentieth century Ernest Shackleton set out to cross Antarctica, but his ship Endurance was crushed by pack ice. His leadership through the ordeal that followed, bringing every man home alive, became a byword for endurance at sea.

title: The Polynesian voyagers
text: Long before European ships reached the Pacific, the Polynesians settled its scattered islands by sailing great distances in open canoes. Reading the stars, swells, winds, and the flight of birds, they navigated across an ocean of vast emptiness.

title: Pytheas of Massalia
text: Pytheas was an ancient Greek explorer who, around the fourth century before our era, sailed from the Mediterranean far into the northern seas. He described tides, the midnight sun, and lands of ice, wonders scarcely believed by those at home.

title: The Norse seafarers
text: The Norse were bold seafarers who, in sturdy open ships, crossed the northern Atlantic to settle Iceland and Greenland and to reach the shores of North America. They navigated by the Sun, the stars, and a close knowledge of the sea.

title: The force of gravity
text: Gravity is the force of attraction between all things that have mass, stronger with greater mass and weaker with distance. It holds us to the Earth, keeps the Moon in its orbit, and governs the motions of the planets and the stars.

title: Newton's first law
text: Newton's first law of motion holds that an object at rest stays at rest, and one in motion keeps moving straight and steady, unless a force acts upon it. This tendency to resist any change of motion is called inertia.

title: Newton's second law
text: Newton's second law relates force, mass, and acceleration: the force needed to change a body's motion grows with both its mass and how sharply its motion changes. A heavier object thus needs a greater push to gain the same speed.

title: Newton's third law
text: Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When a propeller pushes water backward, the water pushes the ship forward, and this principle lies behind every form of propulsion.

title: The speed of light
text: Light travels through empty space at about three hundred thousand kilometres a second, the swiftest speed known and a limit set by nature itself. Even so, light from the Sun takes some eight minutes to reach the Earth.

title: How sound travels
text: Sound is a wave of vibration passing through a material, whether air, water, or solid. It needs a medium to travel and moves faster through denser matter, so sound travels several times faster through water than through air.

title: Sound in water
text: Sound travels through seawater about four times faster than through air and can carry over great distances. This is why whales may call across whole ocean basins and why sonar serves so well for probing the depths of the sea.

title: Refraction of light
text: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium into another, as from air into water. It makes a submerged oar look bent and causes objects seen through water to appear shifted from their true place.

title: The visible spectrum
text: White light is a blend of all the colours of the rainbow, which a prism or the raindrops of a shower can spread into a spectrum. Each colour answers to a different wavelength, from the long red to the short violet.

title: Why the sky is blue
text: The sky looks blue because the molecules of the air scatter the shorter blue rays of sunlight far more than the longer red ones. This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every direction and paints the daytime sky.

title: Why sunsets are red
text: At sunset the light travels a long, slanting path through the air, which scatters away most of the blue. The reds and oranges, less easily scattered, pass through to reach our eyes, and so the low Sun and sky glow warm.

title: The force of magnetism
text: Magnetism is a force by which certain materials, above all iron, draw together or push apart and align with magnetic fields. Every magnet has a north and a south pole, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract.

title: The Earth's magnetic field
text: The Earth behaves like a great magnet, its field made by the churning of molten iron deep in the core. This field guides the compass needle, shields the planet from harmful particles of the Sun, and gives rise to the shimmering auroras.

title: The nature of electricity
text: Electricity is the flow of electric charge, most often carried by electrons moving through a conductor such as metal. Harnessed in circuits, it powers lights, engines, and instruments, and in nature it flashes forth as lightning.

title: Conservation of energy
text: The law of conservation of energy holds that energy cannot be made or destroyed, only changed from one form into another. Heat, motion, light, and electricity are all forms that energy may take as it passes through the world.

title: Heat transfer
text: Heat moves from warmer places to cooler ones in three ways: by conduction through direct contact, by convection through the motion of fluids, and by radiation as unseen rays. Together they carry warmth through the sea, the air, and all the Earth.

title: Pressure and force
text: Pressure is force spread over an area, so the same force presses harder when concentrated on a small area. This is why a sharp point pierces easily and why deep water, bearing over every part of a body, exerts such enormous pressure.

title: Buoyant force in fluids
text: A buoyant force pushes upward on anything set in a fluid, arising because pressure grows with depth and so presses harder on the bottom of an object than on the top. This upward push is what makes swimming and floating possible.

title: The lever
text: A lever is a simple machine, a rigid bar turning on a pivot, that lets a small force move a great load. By choosing where to set the pivot, one trades distance for force, lifting weights far beyond the strength of the naked hand.

title: The pulley
text: A pulley is a wheel with a grooved rim over which a rope runs, used to change the line of a pull or, joined with others, to lessen the effort of raising a load. Aboard ship, blocks of pulleys hoist heavy sails and cargo.

title: The screw
text: The screw is a simple machine, an inclined plane wound about a shaft, that turns rotation into a strong straight-line force. It fastens timbers, lifts water, and, in the form of the propeller, drives ships through the sea.

title: The force of friction
text: Friction is the force that resists the sliding of one surface over another. It slows moving things and wears them down, yet without it we could neither walk nor grasp, and a ship would find no purchase to hold its course.

title: Momentum of a body
text: Momentum is the quantity of motion a body carries, greater for heavier and faster things. A large ship under way has enormous momentum, which is why it cannot stop or turn quickly and must be handled with care and foresight.

title: The barometer
text: A barometer measures the pressure of the air, which falls before stormy weather and rises before fair. By watching its changes, sailors and others could foretell coming storms and calms, reading a warning in the weight of the sky.

title: The thermometer
text: A thermometer measures temperature, commonly by the rise and fall of a liquid such as mercury or alcohol in a narrow tube. As the liquid warms it expands and climbs the scale, giving a reading of how hot or cold a thing may be.

title: Colours of the deep
text: As light sinks into the sea, its colours are absorbed one by one, first the reds, then the yellows and greens, leaving only blue in the depths. This is why the deep glows blue and why red creatures there appear almost black.

title: The rainbow
text: A rainbow appears when sunlight passes through raindrops, which bend and split it into its colours. Each drop acts as a tiny prism, and together the countless drops paint an arc of colour across the sky opposite the Sun.

title: Static and lightning
text: Rubbing certain materials builds up static electricity, the very charge that gathers in storm clouds. When enough has gathered, it leaps across as a spark, and in the sky this sudden discharge appears as a bolt of lightning.

title: Energy from the Sun
text: Nearly all the energy that stirs the living world comes from the Sun. Its light warms the land and sea, drives the winds and currents, lifts water into the sky, and, captured by plants, becomes the food on which life depends.

title: The vacuum
text: A vacuum is a space empty of matter, or nearly so. Sound cannot travel through it for want of a medium, and it presses in on no object, yet it is not truly nothing, for light and other rays pass freely across it.

title: Reflection of light
text: Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface. A smooth mirror throws back a clear image, while a rough surface scatters the light in all directions, which is why most objects can be seen but do not shine like glass.

title: Sound echoes
text: An echo is a sound heard again after it has bounced from a distant surface and returned. By timing how long an echo takes to come back, one may reckon the distance to the surface, the very principle by which sonar sounds the sea.

title: Resonance in vibration
text: Resonance is the way an object vibrates strongly when driven at its own natural rhythm, as a swing pushed in time climbs higher. In the sea it can pile up tides in a bay to great heights and set a moored ship rolling in a matching swell.

title: The atom
text: An atom is the smallest unit of a chemical element that keeps that element's nature. It has a dense central nucleus of protons and neutrons, about which the lighter electrons move, and combinations of atoms make up all ordinary matter.

title: Chemical elements
text: An element is a pure substance made of but one kind of atom, which cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means. About ninety elements occur in nature, from light hydrogen to heavy uranium, and they build every material.

title: The periodic table
text: The periodic table sets the chemical elements in order of their atomic number, gathering those of like nature into columns. Its orderly pattern lets chemists foresee how elements will behave and how they will combine with one another.

title: The element oxygen
text: Oxygen is a colourless gas making up about a fifth of the air and needful to the breathing of most living things. Dissolved in water, it lets fish and other sea creatures breathe, and it readily joins with many other elements.

title: The element hydrogen
text: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe, the chief substance of the stars. On Earth it is seldom found alone but is locked up in water and in a countless multitude of other compounds.

title: The element carbon
text: Carbon is the element at the heart of all known life, able to bond with itself and other atoms into endless chains and rings. It forms the framework of every living tissue and cycles endlessly among the air, the sea, and living things.

title: Common salt
text: Common salt, or sodium chloride, is a compound of the reactive metal sodium and the poisonous gas chlorine, yet together they form a harmless substance vital to life. It dissolves readily in water and gives the sea its saltiness.

title: Acids and bases
text: Acids and bases are chemical opposites; acids release hydrogen ions in water and taste sour, while bases take them up and feel slippery. Combined in the right measure they neutralise each other, forming a salt and water.

title: The pH scale
text: The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a solution is, from strongly acid at low numbers through neutral in the middle to strongly basic at high. Seawater is slightly basic, an important condition for the life it holds.

title: Dissolved gases in the sea
text: Seawater holds dissolved gases, chiefly oxygen and carbon dioxide, traded with the air at the surface. Oxygen sustains the sea's animals, while carbon dioxide feeds the tiny plants and helps set the acidity of the ocean.

title: Carbon dioxide
text: Carbon dioxide is a colourless gas given off by breathing, burning, and decay, and taken up by plants and algae in photosynthesis. The ocean absorbs great quantities of it, making it a key player in the balance of the air.

title: Chemical compounds
text: A compound is a substance formed when two or more elements join in fixed proportion, gaining a nature quite unlike its parts. Water, salt, and carbon dioxide are all compounds, each answering to a definite chemical formula.

title: Evaporation and condensation
text: Evaporation is the passing of a liquid into vapour as its swifter molecules escape into the air, and condensation is the reverse, as vapour cools and returns to liquid. Together they drive the water cycle and the making of cloud and rain.

title: Corrosion and rust
text: Corrosion is the slow chemical attack upon metals by their surroundings, and rust is the familiar reddish result when iron meets oxygen and moisture. Salt water hastens this decay, which is why ships and coastal ironwork corrode so soon.

title: The nature of metals
text: Metals are elements that gleam when polished, conduct heat and electricity, and can be beaten or drawn into shape. Iron, copper, and lead have long served in ships and instruments, though the sea's salt water wears at them without cease.

title: Chemical reactions
text: A chemical reaction is a change in which substances are transformed into others, their atoms rearranged into new combinations. Burning, rusting, and the making of food by plants are all reactions, each releasing or storing energy as it goes.

title: Chemical solutions
text: A solution forms when one substance dissolves evenly in another, as salt does in water, spreading through it so finely that it cannot be seen. Seawater is a solution of many salts and gases, mixed through the whole body of the sea.

title: Crystals in nature
text: A crystal is a solid whose atoms are arranged in an orderly, repeating pattern, giving it flat faces and regular form. Salt left by evaporating seawater grows into small cubic crystals, each a token of the hidden order within.

title: Mixtures of substances
text: A mixture is a blend of substances that keep their own natures and can be parted again by physical means. Seawater is a mixture, its dissolved salts recovered when the water is boiled away, unlike a compound, which is bound together chemically.

title: The Sun
text: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system, a vast sphere of hot gas that pours out light and heat. Its energy drives the water cycle, the winds, and the ocean currents, and sustains nearly all the life on Earth.

title: The Moon
text: The Moon is the Earth's only natural satellite, a rocky world circling us about once a month. Its gravity raises the tides, its phases mark the passing weeks, and its steady light has long guided travellers by night.

title: Phases of the Moon
text: The Moon shows changing phases as it circles the Earth and we see differing amounts of its sunlit half. From new to crescent, half, gibbous, and full, and back again, the whole cycle runs its course in about twenty-nine and a half days.

title: The planets
text: Eight planets circle the Sun, from small rocky Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars to the giant worlds Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Each keeps its own orbit, held in place by the Sun's gravity across enormous reaches of space.

title: The tides and the Moon
text: The Moon's gravity pulls hardest on the water nearest it, raising a bulge of sea, while a second bulge forms on the far side. As the Earth turns beneath these bulges, coasts pass through them, giving rise to the daily tides.

title: The stars
text: Stars are enormous glowing spheres of gas, like our Sun but so far off that they show only as points of light. They shine for millions or billions of years, and their fixed patterns have guided sailors across the seas since antiquity.

title: The constellations
text: Constellations are the patterns people have traced among the stars, dividing the night sky into figures they could name. They have long served as a map of the heavens, helping navigators find their way and mark the turning of the seasons.

title: The North Star
text: Polaris, the North Star, lies almost straight above the Earth's northern pole, so it seems nearly fixed while the other stars wheel about it. For northern sailors it marks true north and reveals their latitude by its height in the sky.

title: Comets in the sky
text: A comet is a small icy body that, when it nears the Sun, warms and sheds gas and dust to form a glowing head and a long tail. Comets travel on stretched orbits, some returning within years and others after many centuries.

title: The Milky Way
text: The Milky Way is the galaxy that holds our Sun and its planets, a vast disc of hundreds of billions of stars. On dark, clear nights it shows as a faint band of light arching across the sky, the mingled glow of distant suns.

title: Solar and lunar eclipses
text: An eclipse happens when one heavenly body passes into the shadow of another. In a solar eclipse the Moon hides the Sun from view, and in a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls across the Moon, dimming its light for a time.

title: Why we have seasons
text: The Earth's axis is tilted with respect to its orbit, so through the year each hemisphere leans in turn toward and away from the Sun. This tilt, not any change in distance, brings the warmth of summer and the cold of winter.

title: Day and night
text: Day and night come about as the Earth turns on its axis about once every twenty-four hours. As it spins, each place moves in turn into the sunlight and then into shadow, giving the endless round of light and darkness.

title: The solar system
text: The solar system is the Sun together with the worlds bound to it by gravity: the planets and their moons, along with countless smaller bodies of rock and ice. All wheel about the Sun, held in their orbits by its far-reaching pull.

title: Meteors and meteorites
text: A meteor is the streak of light seen when a small piece of rock or dust from space burns up as it plunges into the air. Should any of it survive to reach the ground, that surviving stone is called a meteorite.

title: The Earth as a planet
text: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun, a rocky world wrapped in air and largely covered by ocean. Alone among the known worlds it teems with life, its seas and atmosphere kept in a balance fit for living things.

title: Orbits of the heavens
text: An orbit is the curved path a body follows around another under the pull of gravity. The Moon orbits the Earth and the planets orbit the Sun, each balancing its steady fall toward the centre against its forward motion through space.

title: Tides of Sun and Moon
text: Though the Sun is vastly larger than the Moon, it lies far farther off, so its pull upon the tides is the weaker of the two. When Sun and Moon draw in line their pulls combine, and when they cross at right angles they partly cancel.

title: Plate tectonics
text: The Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into great plates that drift slowly over the hot, yielding rock beneath. Where they pull apart, collide, or grind past one another, mountains rise, oceans widen, and earthquakes and volcanoes are born.

title: Sea floor spreading
text: At the mid-ocean ridges, molten rock wells up and hardens into new sea floor, which then spreads outward on either side. This slow conveyor widens the ocean basins over the ages and carries the continents apart.

title: Volcanoes of the Earth
text: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust through which molten rock, gas, and ash escape from below. Many rise from the sea floor, and some build up into islands, while chains of them trace the restless edges of the crustal plates.

title: Earthquakes and faults
text: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground as stress is released when rocks slip along a fault. Those beneath the sea can lift the water above them all at once and set off a tsunami that races across the ocean.

title: The rock cycle
text: Rocks are made, worn down, and made anew through the rock cycle. Molten rock cools into igneous rock, weathering and pressure turn debris into sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure can change either into metamorphic rock.

title: Sedimentary rock
text: Sedimentary rock forms as layers of sand, mud, or the remains of living things settle, pile up, and harden over long ages. Much of it is laid down upon the sea floor, and it often keeps the fossils of ancient sea creatures.

title: The Earth's layers
text: The Earth is built in layers: a thin rocky crust, a thick mantle of hot, slowly flowing rock, a molten outer core, and a solid inner core of iron. Motion within these layers drives the drift of continents and the stirring of the seas.

title: Fossils in the rocks
text: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of living things from long ago, often turned to stone within layers of sediment. They record the history of life and reveal that many creatures now vanished once swam in ancient seas.

title: Erosion by the sea
text: The sea reshapes the coast through erosion, as waves batter the land, wear away cliffs, and carry off sand and stone. Over time this ceaseless work carves caves, arches, and stacks, and shifts whole beaches along the shore.

title: Coral limestone
text: Great beds of limestone have formed from the gathered skeletons of corals and shelled creatures over immense spans of time. Buried and hardened, these remains build the pale stone that may later be raised into hills and mountains.

title: Igneous rock
text: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens, whether slowly deep underground or swiftly at the surface. Much of the ocean floor is made of such rock, poured out at the ridges where new crust is born.

title: Metamorphic rock
text: Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by great heat and pressure deep within the Earth, without fully melting. Its minerals are recrystallised into new forms, giving stone such as marble, born of altered limestone.

title: Weathering of rock
text: Weathering is the slow breaking down of rock where it lies, by wind, water, frost, and living things. It crumbles even hard stone into sand and soil over ages, and the sea and rivers then carry the fragments away.

title: The age of the Earth
text: The Earth is reckoned to be some four and a half billion years old, an age read from the slow decay of certain elements within its rocks. In so vast a span, oceans have formed, continents drifted, and countless forms of life arisen and passed.

title: Islands from the sea
text: Many islands are born of the sea floor itself, thrown up where volcanoes build their cones above the waves. Others are raised where coral grows or where a fall in sea level lays bare the tops of drowned hills.

title: The nature of sand
text: Sand is a loose material of tiny grains, worn from rock or built from the broken shells and skeletons of sea creatures. Waves and currents sort and carry it, heaping it into beaches, bars, and dunes along the shifting edges of the sea.

title: Minerals of the Earth
text: A mineral is a naturally formed solid with a definite chemical make-up and orderly inner structure. Rocks are built of minerals, and the sea itself holds vast stores of dissolved mineral matter gathered from the land over ages.

title: What makes a fish
text: A fish is a cold-blooded animal that lives in water, breathes through gills, and usually bears fins and a body clad in scales. Fish are the most numerous of the backboned animals, filling every watery home from mountain streams to the deep sea.

title: How fish breathe
text: Fish breathe by drawing water in through the mouth and passing it over their gills, feathery structures rich in blood. There the oxygen dissolved in the water is taken up and carbon dioxide given off, before the water flows out through the gill slits.

title: Fish gills
text: Gills are the breathing organs of fish, formed of thin filaments packed with fine blood vessels. Their folded surfaces spread a great area to the passing water, letting the fish draw out the dissolved oxygen it needs to live.

title: The swim bladder
text: Many fish carry a gas-filled swim bladder that lets them govern their buoyancy. By adjusting the gas within it, a fish may hang without effort at a chosen depth, spared the constant swimming that would otherwise keep it from sinking or rising.

title: Fish scales
text: Most fish are clothed in overlapping scales, thin plates of bone or horn that guard the body while letting it bend. A film of slippery mucus over the scales wards off parasites and eases the fish's passage through the water.

title: The lateral line
text: Fish bear a lateral line, a row of sensory pores along each side, that senses faint movements and changes of pressure in the water. Through it they feel currents, prey, predators, and the neighbours swimming beside them in a school.

title: Fish fins
text: A fish's fins steer, steady, and drive it through the water. The tail fin thrusts it forward, the paired side fins allow turning and braking, and the fins along the back and belly keep the body upright and true.

title: Cartilaginous fish
text: Sharks, rays, and their kin are cartilaginous fish, whose skeletons are of tough, springy cartilage rather than bone. This ancient group differs from the bony fish in many ways, among them the lack of a gas-filled swim bladder.

title: Bony fish
text: Bony fish, whose skeletons are of true bone, form by far the largest group of fish, numbering tens of thousands of kinds. From tiny gobies to great tuna, they include nearly all the familiar fish of river, lake, and sea.

title: Cold-blooded fish
text: Most fish are cold-blooded, their body temperature following that of the water around them. This lets them live sparingly, without spending energy to keep warm, though it binds their vigour to the warmth or chill of their surroundings.

title: The flatfish
text: Flatfish such as flounder, sole, and plaice lie upon the sea floor with both eyes on the upper side of the body. Remarkably, they begin life shaped like other fish, and one eye slowly travels across the head as the young fish settles to the bottom.

title: Schooling fish
text: Many fish swim together in schools, moving as one to baffle predators, ease their travel, and better their chance of finding food and mates. Sensing their fellows by sight and by the lateral line, they turn and dart in wonderful unison.

title: The seahorse
text: The seahorse is a curious fish with a horse-like head, a curling tail, and an upright bearing. Among seahorses it is the male that carries the developing young in a pouch upon his body, until they are ready to be loosed into the sea.

title: The eel
text: Eels are long, snake-like fish able to live in both fresh and salt water. Certain eels make astonishing journeys, born far out in the ocean and travelling to rivers to grow, then returning across thousands of kilometres to spawn.

title: The anglerfish
text: The deep-sea anglerfish lures prey with a glowing rod that dangles before its mouth, lit by luminous bacteria. In the darkness of the depths this living lantern draws unwary creatures near enough to be seized in its wide, toothy jaws.

title: The flying fish
text: Flying fish escape their hunters by leaping from the water and gliding on outstretched, wing-like fins. Gathering speed beneath the surface, they break free and can soar for many metres above the waves before slipping back into the sea.

title: The tuna fish
