text: Tuna are large, powerful ocean fish built for speed, with streamlined bodies and crescent tails. Unusual among fish, they can keep parts of their bodies warmer than the water around them, which helps them race across the open sea.

title: The pufferfish
text: The pufferfish defends itself by gulping water to swell into a rounded, sometimes spiny ball too large and awkward for many predators to swallow. Numerous kinds also carry a powerful poison within their bodies as a further shield.

title: The remora
text: The remora is a fish that fixes itself to sharks, turtles, and other large sea creatures by a sucker atop its head. Carried along for nothing, it feeds on scraps and parasites, gaining both a ride and a meal from its host.

title: Fish and eggs
text: Most fish breed by loosing eggs and sperm into the water, where they meet and are fertilised. A single fish may shed thousands or millions of eggs, since only a few of the drifting young will live to reach their growth.

title: The salmon
text: The salmon is a fish that hatches in fresh rivers, journeys down to grow in the sea, and returns as an adult to spawn in the very stream where it was born. To reach it the salmon fights upstream against the current, leaping falls along the way.

title: The cod
text: The cod is a large bottom-dwelling fish of the cold northern seas, long among the most valued of food fishes. Gathering in great numbers over shallow banks, it feeds on smaller fish and shellfish and has fed nations from the sea for ages.

title: The herring
text: The herring is a small, silvery fish of the northern seas that swims in immense schools near the surface. Feeding on drifting plankton and feeding in turn a host of larger creatures, it forms a vital link in the ocean's chain of life.

title: The mackerel
text: The mackerel is a swift, streamlined fish marked with dark bars along its back, roaming the open sea in schools. A tireless swimmer, it hunts smaller fish and plankton and is itself pursued by tuna, dolphins, and seabirds.

title: The moray eel
text: The moray eel lurks by day in crevices among the rocks and reef, its head thrust out and jaws agape. By night it hunts fish and octopuses, and it breathes by opening and closing its mouth to drive water across its gills.

title: The lionfish
text: The lionfish is a striking reef fish arrayed with long, fan-like fins and bold stripes. Beautiful though it is, its spines bear venom, so its finery serves as a warning to any creature that might think to seize it.

title: The sunfish
text: The ocean sunfish is a huge, strange fish shaped almost like a great swimming head, among the heaviest of the bony fishes. It drifts near the surface feeding on jellyfish and often lies on its side, basking in the warmth of the sun.

title: Fish coloration
text: The colours of fish serve many ends. Bright hues may warn of poison or attract a mate, silvery flanks scatter light to hide a fish in open water, and dark backs with pale bellies blend a fish against the depths below and the bright surface above.

title: Deep-sea fishes
text: Fishes of the deep sea are shaped by darkness, cold, and scarcity of food. Many bear glowing lights, wide mouths, and long teeth to seize any rare prey, and some hang nearly still to save the little energy that the depths afford them.

title: The electric eel
text: The electric eel, a fish of South American rivers, can loose a strong electric shock from special organs along its body. It uses this jolt to stun its prey and to defend itself, and the power it wields once puzzled the early students of electricity.

title: Cleaner fish
text: Certain small fish make their living by picking parasites and dead skin from larger fish, which come to be cleaned and hold still while the work is done. Both gain from the bargain: the small fish is fed, and the large one freed of its pests.

title: The sharks
text: Sharks are cartilaginous fish that have swum the seas for hundreds of millions of years. With keen senses, powerful jaws, and many rows of replaceable teeth, they range from tiny kinds to giants and are among the ocean's chief predators.

title: Shark teeth
text: A shark's teeth stand in several rows, and as those in front break or wear away, new teeth move forward to take their place. Over a lifetime a shark may grow and shed many thousands of teeth in this endless succession.

title: Shark senses
text: Sharks are guided by remarkably keen senses, among them a sense of smell that can catch faint traces of blood in the water. Special pores on the snout even sense the tiny electric fields given off by the muscles of hidden prey.

title: The great white shark
text: The great white shark is a large, powerful hunter of cool coastal seas the world over. Armed with rows of serrated teeth and able to sense faint scents and electric fields, it preys chiefly on seals, sea lions, and fish.

title: The whale shark
text: The whale shark is the largest fish in the sea, longer than a bus, yet it feeds gently on tiny plankton and small fish. Cruising slowly through warm waters, it strains its food from the sea, filtering great mouthfuls of water.

title: The hammerhead shark
text: The hammerhead shark takes its name from its broad, flattened head with an eye at each end. This strange shape spreads its senses wider, giving it a broad field of view and a fine ability to find prey buried in the sea floor.

title: Rays and skates
text: Rays and skates are flattened kin of the sharks, with broad, wing-like fins that ripple to move them gracefully along. Many dwell on the sea floor, where their shape lets them lie half-hidden as they hunt shellfish and other prey.

title: The manta ray
text: The manta ray is a giant, gentle relative of the sharks, its wings spanning more than seven metres. Gliding through the open sea, it filters tiny plankton from the water and is harmless to people despite its imposing size.

title: The stingray
text: The stingray is a flat, bottom-dwelling relative of the sharks, armed with a sharp, venomous spine upon its tail. It uses this barb only in defence, lashing out if trodden upon, and otherwise spends its time hunting shellfish on the floor.

title: The electric ray
text: The electric ray can loose a powerful shock from special organs in its body, which it uses to stun its prey and to fend off enemies. The ancients knew of its jolt long before electricity itself was understood.

title: Shark skin
text: A shark's skin is covered in tiny tooth-like scales that make it rough to the touch and cut the drag as the shark swims. This clever design, honed over ages, lets sharks slip through the water with remarkable ease.

title: Why some sharks must swim
text: Some sharks must keep swimming to breathe, driving water over their gills as they go, while others can pump water and rest on the bottom. This need to move helps explain the ceaseless roaming of many of the ocean's great sharks.

title: Shark reproduction
text: Sharks breed in varied ways: some lay tough-cased eggs upon the sea floor, while others bear their young alive after they have grown within the mother. Their offspring are few but well-formed, ready to fend for themselves from the first.

title: The nurse shark
text: The nurse shark is a slow, docile bottom-dweller that spends the day resting in caves and under ledges. By night it roams the reef, sucking up shellfish and small creatures with a strong mouth suited to feeding on the sea floor.

title: The sawfish
text: The sawfish is a strange ray whose long snout is edged with teeth like a saw. It swings this bladed snout to stun small fish and to stir up prey from the muddy bottoms of shallow coastal and river waters where it lives.

title: The tiger shark
text: The tiger shark is a large hunter of warm seas, named for the dark bars that mark the young. Bold and far-ranging, it eats a wide variety of prey, and its powerful, notched teeth let it feed even on turtles and other hard-shelled creatures.

title: Marine mammals
text: Marine mammals such as whales, dolphins, and seals are warm-blooded animals that breathe air, yet pass their lives in or beside the sea. Their forebears returned to the water long ago, and they have since grown wonderfully suited to ocean life.

title: The blue whale
text: The blue whale is the largest animal ever known to have lived, longer than three buses and heavier than many together. For all its bulk it feeds on tiny shrimp-like krill, straining vast swarms of them from the sea through comb-like plates.

title: Baleen whales
text: Baleen whales feed not with teeth but with fringed plates of baleen hanging from the upper jaw. Taking in great mouthfuls of water, they push it out through the baleen, trapping small fish and krill upon the bristly plates within.

title: Toothed whales
text: Toothed whales, including dolphins, porpoises, and the sperm whale, catch fish and squid with their teeth rather than filtering their food. They hunt by sound, sending out clicks and listening for the echoes to find prey in dark water.

title: Whale songs
text: Some whales, above all the humpback, produce long, complex sequences of sound known as songs. These carry far through the water and are thought to play a part in courtship and in the calling of whale to whale across the sea.

title: How whales breathe
text: Whales breathe air through blowholes atop the head, surfacing to blow out a misty spout and draw a fresh breath before diving again. They can hold their breath far longer than land animals, some for well over an hour at a time.

title: The sperm whale
text: The sperm whale is the largest of the toothed whales and dives deeper than almost any other mammal in pursuit of squid. Its great blunt head holds a waxy store once prized by whalers and may help focus the sounds it uses to hunt.

title: The dolphins
text: Dolphins are small, clever toothed whales known for their play and their close-knit groups. They hunt fish and squid by echolocation, chase and leap through the waves, and keep up a lively converse of whistles and clicks.

title: Hunting by echolocation
text: Toothed whales and dolphins hunt by echolocation, sending out rapid clicks and listening for the echoes that return from objects. From these returning sounds they build a detailed picture of their surroundings, even in dark or murky water.

title: Seals and sea lions
text: Seals and sea lions are marine mammals that swim gracefully with flippers, yet must return to land or ice to rest and rear their young. A layer of blubber keeps them warm in cold seas as they hunt fish, squid, and shellfish.

title: The walrus
text: The walrus is a large marine mammal of Arctic seas, easily known by its long ivory tusks and bristling whiskers. It uses its tusks to haul out onto the ice and its sensitive whiskers to find clams and other shellfish on the sea floor.

title: The sea otter
text: The sea otter is a marine mammal that floats on its back among the kelp, using stones to crack open shellfish on its chest. Lacking blubber, it depends on its dense fur, the thickest of any animal, to keep warm in cold coastal seas.

title: Dugongs and manatees
text: Dugongs and manatees, sometimes called sea cows, are gentle marine mammals that graze on underwater plants in warm coastal waters. Slow and harmless, they may well have given rise to old sailors' tales of mermaids.

title: Whale migration
text: Many whales migrate over immense distances between cold feeding grounds rich in food and warm waters where they breed and bear their young. These journeys, among the longest of any animal, may cover thousands of kilometres each way.

title: Whale blubber
text: Blubber is the thick layer of fat beneath the skin of whales, seals, and other marine mammals. It shields them from the cold of the sea, stores energy for long journeys, and lends their bodies a smooth, streamlined form.

title: The narwhal
text: The narwhal is an Arctic toothed whale, the male bearing a long, spiralled tusk that is in truth an overgrown tooth. This remarkable ivory spear, sometimes more than two metres long, once passed in Europe for the horn of the unicorn.

title: The orca
text: The orca, or killer whale, is the largest of the dolphin family and a formidable hunter of the sea. Living in tight family groups, orcas work together to take fish, seals, and even other whales, and pass their skills from one generation to the next.

title: The humpback whale
text: The humpback whale is a large baleen whale famed for its long flippers, its breaching leaps, and the haunting songs of the males. It feeds by lunging through swarms of krill and small fish, sometimes herding them with curtains of rising bubbles.

title: The porpoise
text: The porpoise is a small, shy toothed whale, kin to the dolphin but blunter of snout and more retiring in its ways. It keeps mostly to coastal waters, where it hunts fish quietly and seldom leaps or plays about ships as dolphins do.

title: Warm blood in cold seas
text: Marine mammals keep a steady, warm body in the chill of the sea by their blubber, their dense fur, or both, and by a body built to hold heat. Their limbs are arranged so that warm blood flowing outward warms the cold blood returning.

title: The leopard seal
text: The leopard seal is a lithe and powerful hunter of the cold southern seas, named for the spots upon its coat. With its long jaws and sharp teeth it preys on penguins, fish, and even other seals among the drifting ice of Antarctica.

title: The elephant seal
text: The elephant seal is the largest of all the seals, the great males bearing a swollen, trunk-like snout. Superb divers, they plunge to remarkable depths in search of fish and squid, holding their breath far longer than most other mammals.

title: The cephalopods
text: Cephalopods are a group of clever molluscs that includes the octopus, squid, cuttlefish, and nautilus. With large brains, keen eyes, and grasping arms or tentacles, they are among the most intelligent of all the animals without a backbone.

title: The octopus
text: The octopus is a soft-bodied cephalopod with eight arms lined with suckers and a keen, curious mind. It can change its colour and texture to melt into its surroundings, squeeze through narrow gaps, and even work out simple puzzles for food.

title: The squid
text: The squid is a swift cephalopod with a streamlined body, eight arms, and two longer tentacles for seizing prey. It swims by drawing water into its body and forcing it out through a funnel, jetting backward through the sea.

title: The giant squid
text: The giant squid is a deep-sea cephalopod that grows to great length, with enormous eyes suited to the dim depths. Rarely seen alive, it long fed sailors' tales of sea monsters, and it is hunted in the deep by the sperm whale.

title: The cuttlefish
text: The cuttlefish is a cephalopod famed for its power to change colour, flashing patterns across its skin to signal and to hide. Within its body lies the cuttlebone, a chambered internal shell that helps it govern its buoyancy.

title: The nautilus
text: The nautilus is an ancient cephalopod that lives within a lovely coiled, chambered shell. By adjusting the gas in its sealed chambers it controls its buoyancy, and it has kept much the same form for many millions of years.

title: Cephalopod ink
text: Squid, octopuses, and cuttlefish can shoot out a cloud of dark ink to confuse and screen themselves from their enemies. The inky screen hangs in the water while the animal jets away to safety in some other direction.

title: Colour change in cephalopods
text: Cephalopods change colour by means of tiny sacs of pigment in the skin that they can spread or draw in at will. In an instant they can flush with colour, vanish into the background, or send rippling signals across their whole bodies.

title: Jet propulsion
text: Squid and octopuses move by jet propulsion, drawing water into a cavity and squirting it out through a narrow funnel. By aiming the funnel they can dart in any direction, and squid can shoot backward through the sea with great speed.

title: Cephalopod eyes
text: Cephalopods have large, well-made eyes that in some ways resemble our own, though they arose quite separately. These sharp eyes serve their active, hunting life and rank among the finest in the whole world of creatures without a backbone.

title: Cephalopod arms and suckers
text: The arms of an octopus or squid are lined with suckers that grip prey, rock, and any surface with remarkable strength and delicacy. The octopus can taste as well as touch through its suckers, exploring its world with each of its supple arms.

title: The vampire squid
text: The vampire squid is a small, deep-sea creature, neither true squid nor octopus, that dwells in dark, oxygen-poor waters. It drifts gently rather than darting, and when alarmed it can turn its webbed arms up over itself like a spiked cloak.

title: The crustaceans
text: Crustaceans are a vast group of animals with jointed legs and a hard outer shell, among them crabs, lobsters, shrimp, and barnacles. Most live in water, where they range from microscopic drifters to the great crabs of the deep.

title: The crab
text: A crab is a crustacean with a broad, flattened body, a hard shell, and a pair of pincers. It walks sideways on its jointed legs, and like other crustaceans it must shed its shell and grow a new one as its body enlarges.

title: The lobster
text: The lobster is a large crustacean with a long body, a strong tail, and powerful claws. It roams the sea floor by night in search of food and can live for many years, growing slowly and moulting its shell as it grows.

title: Shrimp and prawns
text: Shrimp and prawns are small, swimming crustaceans with slender bodies and many delicate legs. Abundant through all the seas, they form an important link in the ocean's food webs, feeding on tiny scraps and in turn feeding countless fish.

title: The barnacles
text: Barnacles are crustaceans that pass their adult lives fixed to rocks, ships, and even whales, sealed within a hard shell. From this small fortress they reach out feathery legs to sweep tiny food from the water flowing by.

title: Moulting the shell
text: Crustaceans and many other creatures with hard outer shells must moult to grow, casting off the old shell and forming a larger one. During this vulnerable time, before the new shell hardens, the animal hides away from its enemies.

title: The tiny krill
text: Krill are small, shrimp-like crustaceans that swarm in immense numbers in the cold seas. They feed on drifting plankton and are themselves the chief food of great whales, seals, penguins, and a host of fish and seabirds.

title: The hermit crab
text: The hermit crab has a soft, curled body that it guards by dwelling within an empty snail shell. As it grows it must seek out ever larger shells to move into, carrying its borrowed home along wherever it goes.

title: The crustacean shell
text: A crustacean's body is guarded by an exoskeleton, a hard outer casing that also anchors its muscles. Stiffened in many kinds with lime drawn from the sea, this armour shields the soft body within but must be shed for the animal to grow.

title: The mantis shrimp
text: The mantis shrimp is a small but formidable crustacean armed with clubs or spears that it strikes with astonishing speed. Its blow can crack the shell of a crab or snail, and its eyes are among the most intricate in the animal kingdom.

title: The spider crab
text: The spider crab bears long, slender legs that give it a spidery look, and some kinds span a great reach from claw to claw. Slow and gentle, it wanders the sea floor and often decks its shell with bits of weed and sponge for disguise.

title: The copepods
text: Copepods are tiny crustaceans that drift in vast numbers among the plankton of the sea. Though each is barely visible, together they are among the most abundant animals on Earth and a chief food of many small fish and young of larger ones.

title: The horseshoe crab
text: The horseshoe crab is not a true crab but an ancient sea creature, kin rather to spiders, little changed for hundreds of millions of years. Beneath its rounded shell it walks the shallow sea floor and comes ashore in numbers to lay its eggs.

title: The molluscs
text: Molluscs are soft-bodied animals, many guarded by a shell, forming one of the largest groups in the animal kingdom. Among them are snails, clams, oysters, and mussels, as well as the clever octopuses and squid of the open sea.

title: The bivalve molluscs
text: Bivalves such as clams, oysters, mussels, and scallops are molluscs whose bodies are held between two hinged shells. Many draw in water and strain tiny food from it, quietly filtering the sea as they feed.

title: The oyster
text: The oyster is a bivalve mollusc that lives fixed to hard surfaces, filtering its food from the water. Some kinds make pearls, formed as the animal coats an intruding grain with the same lustrous stuff that lines its shell.

title: How pearls form
text: A pearl grows when a grain of sand or other irritant lodges within an oyster or mussel. To guard itself, the animal wraps the intruder in layer upon layer of smooth nacre, the same substance that lines its shell, building a lustrous pearl.

title: Sea snails
text: Sea snails are molluscs that bear a coiled shell and creep upon a muscular foot. They graze on algae or hunt other small creatures, and their beautiful shells wash up in endless variety along the world's shores.

title: The giant clam
text: The giant clam is the largest of the bivalve molluscs, its heavy shells growing more than a metre across. It lives upon coral reefs and gains much of its food from tiny algae that dwell within its colourful, fleshy mantle.

title: Mollusc shells
text: Many molluscs build a hard shell of lime drawn from the sea, secreted by the soft fold of tissue called the mantle. The shell grows with the animal and guards its tender body, and the finest are prized for their form and colour.

title: The chiton
text: The chiton is a mollusc that clings to rocks beneath a shell of eight overlapping plates, which let it bend and hold fast to uneven surfaces. It grazes on algae with a rasping tongue and can curl into a ball if it is dislodged.

title: The scallop
text: The scallop is a bivalve that, unlike most of its kin, can swim by clapping its two shells together to jet through the water. Rows of tiny eyes along the edge of its mantle keep watch for the shadow of an approaching enemy.

title: The mussel
text: The mussel is a bivalve that anchors itself to rocks and pilings by tough threads it spins, gathering in dense beds along the shore. Filtering its food from the water, it endures the pounding surf and the bare spells between the tides.

title: The sea slug
text: Sea slugs are molluscs that have lost the shell of their snail kin, and many wear instead the most brilliant colours in the sea. Some feed on stinging anemones and store the stings, turning their prey's weapons to their own defence.

title: The cone snail
text: The cone snail is a hunting sea snail housed in a smooth, patterned shell. It strikes its prey with a tiny venomous dart, and the venom of some kinds is potent enough to make the cone snail dangerous to handle carelessly.

title: The abalone
text: The abalone is a large sea snail whose single, ear-shaped shell clings tightly to rock. Grazing on seaweed, it lines the inside of its shell with shining mother-of-pearl, long prized for its beauty by those who gather it from the shore.

title: Living coral
text: Coral is built by tiny animals called polyps, kin to the jellyfish, that live in colonies and lay down skeletons of lime. Over ages the stony skeletons of countless generations gather to form the great reefs of the warm seas.

title: The coral polyp
text: A coral polyp is a small, soft-bodied animal, like a tiny anemone, that dwells in a cup of its own making. It catches food with stinging tentacles, and reef-building polyps also share their flesh with tiny algae that help to feed them.

title: Coral reefs
text: Coral reefs are vast structures built by colonies of coral over thousands of years in warm, shallow seas. Teeming with fish and other creatures, they rank among the richest and most colourful of habitats, and are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea.

title: The Great Barrier Reef
text: The Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Australia is the largest coral reef system in the world, stretching more than two thousand kilometres. Built by countless tiny coral animals, it shelters an astonishing variety of marine life.

title: Coral and algae
text: Reef-building corals live in partnership with tiny algae within their tissues. The algae harvest sunlight and share the food they make, while the coral gives them shelter, a bond that lets reefs flourish in otherwise nutrient-poor waters.

title: Coral bleaching
text: When corals are stressed, most often by water that is too warm, they cast out the tiny algae living within them and turn pale, an event called bleaching. Robbed of their partners' food, the corals weaken and may die if the stress persists.

title: Types of coral reef
text: Coral reefs take several forms: fringing reefs that hug the shore, barrier reefs parted from land by a lagoon, and ring-shaped atolls that enclose a lagoon of their own. Darwin explained how one may in time change into another.

title: Sea anemones
text: Sea anemones are soft-bodied kin of the coral and jellyfish that anchor to rocks and wave their stinging tentacles to catch passing prey. Some share a curious friendship with small fish that shelter unharmed among their tentacles.

title: The clownfish and anemone
text: The clownfish lives among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone, guarded from harm by a special coating on its skin. It gains shelter from its enemies, while the anemone gains from the fish's presence, in a bond of mutual help.

title: Reef fish
text: The reef teems with fish of every hue, from the darting damselfish to the grazing parrotfish and the hovering angelfish. Their bright colours help them know one another, warn of danger, or blend among the corals in the shifting light.

title: The parrotfish
text: The parrotfish takes its name from the beak-like plates with which it scrapes algae from coral. Grinding the hard coral as it feeds, it passes the rock as fine sand, and so a single parrotfish helps make the pale sand of tropical shores.

title: Cold-water corals
text: Not all corals need warm, sunlit seas; some build reefs in cold, dark waters far below the reach of light. Lacking the sunlit algae of shallow reefs, they feed instead by catching the tiny creatures drifting past in the deep currents.

title: Soft corals
text: Not all corals build stony reefs; the soft corals bear no hard skeleton but sway in the current like plants, held up by tiny needles of lime within their flesh. In fans, whips, and plumes they add their forms to the living tapestry of the reef.

title: Brain coral
text: Brain coral takes its name from its rounded form and the winding, grooved surface that recalls the folds of a brain. A single such boulder is the work of countless tiny polyps, laid down slowly over many long years of patient growth.

title: The drifting plankton
text: Plankton are the small, often microscopic organisms that drift with the ocean currents, unable to swim against them. Though tiny, they are the foundation of nearly all marine life, feeding creatures great and small throughout the sea.

title: The phytoplankton
text: Phytoplankton are the tiny, plant-like drifters of the sea that harness sunlight to make their food, as plants do on land. They form the base of the ocean's food web and give off a great share of the oxygen we breathe.

title: The zooplankton
text: Zooplankton are the small drifting animals of the sea, from single-celled creatures to tiny shrimp and the young of larger animals. Grazing on the phytoplankton, they in turn feed fish and whales, forming a vital link in the food web.

title: The diatoms
text: Diatoms are microscopic phytoplankton encased in delicate shells of glassy silica, wrought in an endless variety of intricate shapes. Drifting in their countless billions, they are among the ocean's chief makers of food and oxygen.

title: Plankton and oxygen
text: The tiny phytoplankton of the sea produce a great portion of the world's oxygen through photosynthesis. Though each is invisibly small, together across the vast oceans they help sustain the breathable air of the whole planet.

title: Plankton blooms
text: When conditions favour them, phytoplankton can multiply explosively into a bloom that colours the water and may be seen from far above. Such blooms feed a surge of ocean life, but as they fade and decay they can rob the water of its oxygen.

title: Krill and the food web
text: Tiny krill graze upon the drifting phytoplankton and are eaten in turn by fish, seabirds, seals, and the greatest whales. By passing the energy of the smallest plants to the largest of animals, they form a crucial link in the ocean food web.

title: The dinoflagellates
text: Dinoflagellates are tiny drifting organisms, some plant-like and some more like animals, that swim with whip-like tails. Certain kinds glow in the dark, lighting the sea when it is stirred, and others multiply into blooms that colour the water red.

title: The foraminifera
text: Foraminifera are tiny single-celled drifters of the sea that build delicate chambered shells of lime. When they die, their shells sink and settle over ages into thick beds of chalk and ooze upon the floor of the deep ocean.

title: The plankton net
text: Naturalists study the drifting life of the sea by towing a fine-meshed net behind a ship to strain the plankton from the water. From a single haul may come a teeming multitude of tiny creatures, the hidden foundation of all ocean life.

title: The jellyfish
text: Jellyfish are soft, drifting animals with bell-shaped bodies and trailing tentacles, made largely of water. Among the most ancient of animals, they pulse gently through the sea and catch their prey with stinging tentacles.

title: How jellyfish sting
text: A jellyfish's tentacles bear countless tiny stinging cells, each holding a coiled thread that fires like a harpoon at a touch. These threads inject venom to numb small creatures, which the tentacles then draw in toward the mouth.

title: The jellyfish life cycle
text: Many jellyfish pass through two very different stages: a small polyp fixed to the sea floor, and the free-swimming bell we know as a jellyfish. From the anchored polyp, young medusae bud away to drift off and grow into adults.

title: The Portuguese man o' war
text: The Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish but is truly a colony of specialised creatures living together as one. A gas-filled float carries it upon the wind while long stinging tentacles trail below to catch fish.

title: The box jellyfish
text: The box jellyfish, named for its cube-shaped bell, bears some of the most potent venom in the sea. Trailing long tentacles, it swims more purposefully than most jellyfish and is much feared in the warm waters where it lives.

title: Comb jellies
text: Comb jellies are delicate, transparent sea creatures that move by beating rows of tiny paddle-like combs. As these ripple, they scatter light into shimmering rainbows, and unlike the true jellyfish, comb jellies do not sting.

title: The lion's mane jellyfish
text: The lion's mane is among the largest of jellyfish, its broad bell trailing a great mass of fine tentacles like a flowing mane. It drifts in the cold northern seas, ensnaring small creatures in the long, stinging streamers that hang beneath it.

title: Jellyfish as drifters
text: Though a jellyfish can pulse its bell to rise or sink, it is far too weak to swim against the sea and so drifts largely at the mercy of the currents. Gathered by wind and tide, jellyfish may crowd together in great swarms upon the water.

title: The echinoderms
text: Echinoderms are a group of spiny-skinned sea animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and sea cucumbers. Built on a fivefold symmetry and found only in the sea, they move by means of countless tiny water-filled tube feet.

title: The starfish
text: The starfish, or sea star, is an echinoderm that usually bears five arms about a central body. It creeps along on rows of tiny tube feet and can regrow a lost arm, and some feed by pushing the stomach out to digest prey outside the body.

title: The sea urchin
text: The sea urchin is a round, spiny echinoderm that grazes on algae with a curious five-toothed mouth on its underside. Its spines can move, and beneath them lie the same tiny tube feet that all echinoderms use to grip and creep.

title: The sea cucumber
text: The sea cucumber is a soft, sausage-shaped echinoderm that creeps along the sea floor, feeding on the fine debris of the bottom. Some can eject their inner organs to distract a predator, and later grow them anew.

title: Tube feet
text: Echinoderms move and grip by means of tube feet, tiny flexible projections worked by an inner system of water-filled canals. Pumping water in and out, the animal extends, anchors, and pulls with hundreds of these small hydraulic feet.

title: The brittle star
text: The brittle star is a kin of the starfish with a small central disc and long, slender, snake-like arms. It moves far more nimbly than a starfish, writhing its arms to creep, and if seized it readily casts one off to make its escape.

title: Regeneration in sea stars
text: Starfish have a striking power of regeneration, regrowing arms lost to a predator or mishap. In some kinds a single severed arm, if it keeps part of the central body, can even grow into a whole new animal in time.

title: The sand dollar
text: The sand dollar is a flattened kin of the sea urchin that lives half-buried in sandy sea floors. Clad in fine, short spines in life, its bleached round shell, marked with a five-petalled star, is often found cast up along the shore.

title: The crown-of-thorns starfish
text: The crown-of-thorns is a large, many-armed starfish covered in venomous spines that feeds on living coral. When its numbers swell it can strip whole stretches of reef, and so its comings and goings are watched with care.

title: The feather star
text: The feather star is an echinoderm that spreads many feathery arms to strain drifting food from the water. Though some kinds cling in one place, others can creep or even swim, waving their plumed arms as they move about the reef.

title: Hydrothermal vents
text: Hydrothermal vents are cracks in the deep sea floor where water heated by the Earth's inner fire gushes out, laden with minerals. Around them thrives a strange community of life that draws its energy not from sunlight but from chemicals.

title: Life without sunlight
text: At hydrothermal vents in the lightless deep, whole communities live without the Sun. Special bacteria draw energy from chemicals in the venting water, and on this chemical harvest feed tube worms, clams, and creatures found nowhere else.

title: Giant tube worms
text: Giant tube worms cluster around deep-sea hydrothermal vents, growing to great length within white tubes. Lacking mouth or gut, they harbour bacteria within their bodies that feed them from the chemicals of the vent water.

title: Feeding by chemosynthesis
text: Chemosynthesis is the making of food from chemicals rather than from sunlight. In the dark deep sea, certain bacteria harness the energy locked in substances rising from the vents, and on this hidden bounty rest whole communities of animals.

title: Black smokers
text: Black smokers are hydrothermal vents that spew dark, mineral-laden water so hot it would boil at the surface, kept liquid only by the crushing pressure of the deep. As the hot water meets the cold sea, its minerals settle into towering chimneys.

title: The deep-sea floor
text: The floor of the deep sea is a cold, dark, high-pressure world, yet far from lifeless. Strange fish, crawling creatures, and countless burrowers make their living from the sparse rain of food that drifts down from the sunlit waters above.

title: Marine snow
text: Marine snow is the steady drift of tiny particles, the remains of plankton and other organisms, that sinks from the sunlit surface into the deep. This gentle fall of food sustains much of the life in the dark waters far below.

title: Deep-sea gigantism
text: Some creatures of the cold, dark deep grow to surprising size, a tendency called deep-sea gigantism. Giant squid, huge isopods, and long-lived deep-water animals reach dimensions far greater than their kin in warmer, shallower seas.

title: Pressure-adapted life
text: Animals of the deep sea are built to bear pressures that would crush surface creatures. Wanting any air-filled spaces and made largely of water and yielding tissue, their bodies feel little strain from the great weight of the sea above.

title: The cold seeps
text: At cold seeps on the deep sea floor, chemicals rise gently from the sediment without the searing heat of the vents. There too, bacteria draw energy from these chemicals and nourish clusters of clams, worms, and other patient deep-sea life.

title: Whale falls
text: When a great whale dies and sinks to the deep sea floor, its carcass becomes a feast that sustains a whole community for years. Scavengers strip the flesh, and in time even the bones nourish creatures able to live upon them.

title: The isopods of the deep
text: In the cold, dark deep some isopods, kin of the wood louse and the pill bug, grow to a great size undreamed of in their tiny land relatives. Armoured and many-legged, they creep the sea floor, scavenging whatever food sinks from above.

title: Living light in the sea
text: Bioluminescence is the making of light by living things, through a chemical reaction within their bodies. Common in the dark ocean, it serves to lure prey, startle enemies, attract mates, and light the way where the Sun never reaches.

title: The glowing sea
text: On some nights the sea itself seems to glow, sparkling wherever it is stirred. This living light comes from countless tiny plankton that flash when disturbed, trailing brightness behind ships, oars, and the bodies of swimming creatures.

title: Lures of the deep
text: In the lightless depths, many animals use their own glow to draw prey close. The anglerfish dangles a shining bait before its jaws, and others flash and gleam to bring curious creatures within reach of their waiting mouths.

title: How living light is made
text: Living light is usually made when a substance called luciferin reacts with oxygen, aided by a matching agent. The reaction gives off its energy almost wholly as light rather than heat, so the glow is cool and wastes little warmth.

title: Hiding by counterillumination
text: Some deep-sea animals glow softly on their undersides to hide themselves, a trick called counterillumination. By matching the faint light filtering from above, they erase their own silhouette from the eyes of predators lurking below.

title: Glowing plankton
text: Certain tiny plankton flash with light when the water around them is disturbed, so that a breaking wave or a passing swimmer sets the sea aglow. The sudden flash may startle a grazer or draw a larger hunter down upon the one that troubles them.

title: The lanternfish
text: The lanternfish is a small fish of the twilight and midnight depths, its body studded with rows of tiny light organs. It rises toward the surface by night to feed and sinks again by day, and its glow may help its kind to keep together.

title: Marine migration
text: Many sea creatures migrate over great distances to feed, to breed, or to seek warmer or cooler water. Whales, fish, turtles, and seabirds all make such journeys, guided by the Sun, the stars, the currents, and the Earth's magnetic field.

title: The vertical migration
text: Each night, vast numbers of small sea animals rise from the twilight depths toward the surface to feed, sinking again by day to hide in the dark. This daily vertical migration is the greatest movement of living things upon the planet.

title: Ocean food webs
text: In the ocean the Sun's energy is caught by tiny drifting plants and passed along a web of feeding relations. Small grazers eat the plants, larger animals eat the grazers, and so the energy flows upward to the greatest hunters of the sea.

title: The base of the food web
text: At the base of nearly every ocean food web are the phytoplankton, tiny drifters that make food from sunlight. All the animal life of the sea, from the least fish to the greatest whale, rests in the end upon these unseen plants.

title: Predators and prey
text: In the sea, as on land, predators hunt prey, and the balance between them shapes whole communities. The number of hunters depends on the plenty of their food, and the pressure of hunting in turn holds the numbers of prey in check.

title: Filter feeders
text: Filter feeders strain small food from the water rather than chase it. From tiny barnacles and clams to the great baleen whales and whale sharks, they sieve immense quantities of water to gather the plankton and small creatures within.

title: Sea turtles
text: Sea turtles are ancient reptiles that pass their lives in the ocean, coming to land only to lay their eggs on the beaches where they themselves hatched. They navigate across whole oceans, guided in part by the Earth's magnetic field.

title: The seabirds
text: Seabirds such as gulls, albatrosses, and penguins win their living from the sea, diving, plunging, or skimming to catch fish and other prey. Some wander the open ocean for months on end, returning to land only in order to breed.

title: The albatross
text: The albatross is a great seabird with the longest wingspan of any bird, able to glide for hours over the ocean with scarce a beat of its wings. It spends most of its life at sea, coming to remote islands only to nest and rear its young.

title: Kelp forests
text: Kelp forests are underwater groves of giant seaweed that grow swiftly toward the light in cool, clear coastal seas. Their swaying fronds shelter a rich community of fish, otters, and countless smaller creatures among their stems.

title: River estuaries
text: An estuary is where a river meets the sea, mingling fresh and salt water. Sheltered and rich in nutrients, estuaries serve as nurseries for many fish and shellfish and as gathering places for great numbers of birds.

title: The mangroves
text: Mangroves are trees that grow along tropical shores, their tangled roots standing in salt water. Their sheltered thickets guard the coast from storms and waves and serve as nurseries for young fish, crabs, and countless other creatures.

title: Seagrass meadows
text: Seagrasses are flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal waters, forming underwater meadows. They shelter young fish, feed grazers such as turtles and dugongs, and help hold the sea floor in place against the moving currents.

title: The tide pool
text: A tide pool is a pocket of seawater left among the rocks when the tide goes out. In this small world crabs, anemones, snails, and little fish must endure the changing conditions until the returning sea covers them once more.

title: Symbiosis in the sea
text: Symbiosis is a close partnership between different kinds of living things, and the sea abounds in it. Corals share their tissues with algae, clownfish shelter among anemones, and cleaner fish tend larger fish, each partner gaining from the bond.

title: Camouflage in the sea
text: Many sea creatures hide by blending with their surroundings. Flatfish match the sea floor, cuttlefish shift their colours in a moment, and countless small animals wear patterns that break up their shape against rock, sand, or weed.

title: The penguin
text: The penguin is a seabird that has given up flight for a life in the water, its wings become flippers for swimming. Clad in dense, waterproof feathers and a layer of fat, it dives after fish and squid in the cold seas of the far south.

title: The seaweeds
text: Seaweeds are the algae of the sea, from tiny films to the giant kelps, growing where light reaches through the water. Anchored to rock rather than rooted in soil, they make their food from sunlight and shelter a multitude of small creatures.

title: The food pyramid of the sea
text: The living matter of the sea is arranged like a pyramid: a broad base of tiny plants, a smaller mass of grazers above, fewer hunters above them, and fewest of all the great predators at the top. Each level feeds on the one below.

title: Sea birds and fish stocks
text: Great flocks of seabirds gather where fish are plentiful, and their presence has long guided fishermen to the shoals. Where the sea's fish thrive, the birds thrive with them, and their numbers rise and fall with the harvest of the water.

title: The marine iguana
text: The marine iguana of the Galapagos is the only lizard that feeds in the sea, diving to graze on algae from the rocks below. Cold-blooded, it must bask in the sun to warm itself again after its plunge into the chill of the water.

title: Migratory fish
text: Some fish undertake long migrations, journeying between the waters where they feed and those where they breed. Guided by currents, temperature, and other cues, tuna, herring, and their like travel far across the sea in their yearly rounds.

title: Marine biodiversity
text: The ocean holds an immense variety of life, from microscopic plankton to the greatest whales, filling every depth and habitat. This richness, built over ages, upholds the balance of the sea and the countless bonds among its creatures.

title: The peril of overfishing
text: Overfishing happens when fish are taken faster than they can breed, so that their numbers fall. It can unbalance whole marine communities, for the loss of one kind of fish touches all the creatures that fed on it or that it once fed upon.

title: Ocean pollution
text: Pollution harms the sea when hurtful substances enter it from the land, the rivers, and the air. Waste, chemicals, and drifting refuse can poison marine life, foul the shores, and disturb the delicate balance of ocean communities.

title: Nutrients and the food chain
text: Nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus feed the tiny plants at the base of ocean life. In balance they nourish the sea, but in excess, washed from the land, they can spur blooms that later decay and rob the water of its oxygen.

title: Marine protected areas
text: Marine protected areas are stretches of sea set apart to shelter their life from harm. Within them fishing and other pressures may be limited, so that fish can grow and multiply and damaged habitats be given time to recover.

title: The carbon cycle in the sea
text: The ocean plays a great part in the carbon cycle, absorbing carbon dioxide from the air at its surface. Tiny plants take it up in photosynthesis, and much of it sinks slowly into the deep, making the sea a vast storehouse of carbon.

title: Ocean acidification
text: As the sea absorbs more carbon dioxide, its waters grow slightly more acidic. This change makes it harder for corals, shellfish, and other creatures to build their shells and skeletons of lime, threatening the balance of ocean life.

title: The importance of the ocean
text: The ocean shapes the whole living world. It stores heat and moderates the climate, drives the winds and the rains, makes much of the air's oxygen, and feeds and sustains an untold multitude of living things.

title: Coral reefs at risk
text: Coral reefs, among the richest of habitats, are sensitive to changes in their waters. Warming seas, pollution, and rising acidity can weaken or kill the corals, and with them the vast communities of life the reefs support.

title: Keystone species
text: A keystone species holds an influence over its community far greater than its numbers alone would suggest. The sea otter is one such creature, for by preying on sea urchins it guards the kelp forests that shelter countless other animals.

title: Habitat loss in the sea
text: As coasts are built upon and wetlands drained, the sea loses habitats that shelter its young life. Mangroves, marshes, and seagrass meadows serve as nurseries, and their loss weakens the fisheries and the coasts that depend upon them.

title: Sustainable fishing
text: Fishing can be carried on without ruin if no more is taken than the sea can replace. By sparing the young, resting depleted grounds, and setting limits on the catch, fishers may draw a lasting harvest from the water year upon year.

title: How photosynthesis works
text: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and algae use the energy of sunlight to make food from carbon dioxide and water, giving off oxygen as they do. It is the foundation of nearly all life, on the land and in the sea alike.

title: The cell
text: The cell is the smallest unit of life, the building block of every living thing. Some creatures are but a single cell, while a large animal is built of many billions, each carrying out in its small way the tasks of living.

title: Cold-blooded and warm-blooded
text: Warm-blooded animals such as mammals and birds keep a steady body warmth by their own heat, while cold-blooded animals such as fish and reptiles take on the temperature of their surroundings. Each way of life is suited to its own conditions.

title: Adaptation in nature
text: Adaptation is the way living things grow suited to their surroundings over many generations, as those best fitted to survive leave the most young. The streamlined shape of a fish and the thick blubber of a whale are such adaptations.

title: The study of ecology
text: Ecology is the study of how living things relate to one another and to their surroundings. It traces the flow of energy and matter through communities of life and the delicate balances that bind predator to prey and creature to home.

title: The food chain
text: A food chain follows the passage of energy from one living thing to the next as each is eaten in turn. Beginning with plants that catch sunlight, it climbs through grazers to hunters, though in nature these chains cross into tangled webs.

title: Natural selection
text: Natural selection is the process by which living things better suited to their surroundings tend to survive and leave more young, passing on their traits. Over long ages it shapes the endless forms of life, each fitted to its way of living.

title: Reptiles of the sea
text: A few reptiles have taken to the sea, among them sea turtles, sea snakes, and the marine iguana. Though they breathe air and most lay their eggs on land, they are well suited to life in the water and range far along the warm coasts.

title: The amphibians
text: Amphibians such as frogs and salamanders live partly in water and partly on land, beginning life in the water and often breathing through their moist skin. Few can bear salt, so they belong to fresh waters rather than to the sea.

title: The variety of life
text: Living things come in astonishing variety, from tiny microbes to great whales, filling every corner of land, air, and sea. Naturalists group and name them to make sense of this abundance and to trace the ties of kinship among them.

title: Warm and cold currents and life
text: The mingling of warm and cold currents makes some of the richest fishing grounds in the sea. Cold water rising from below brings up nutrients, and where it meets the warmth and light of the surface, life multiplies in great abundance.

title: Classification of living things
text: Naturalists sort living things into a nested order of groups, from broad kingdoms down to the single kind, or species. This ordering, refined over ages, reveals the kinship of creatures and helps make sense of the vast diversity of life.

title: A species of life
text: A species is a kind of living thing whose members share a common form and can breed together to bring forth young of their own kind. It is the basic unit by which naturalists reckon and name the countless forms of life in the sea and on land.

title: Sea ice
text: Sea ice forms as the surface of the ocean freezes in the cold of the polar regions. Because much of the salt is left behind as it forms, sea ice is far less salty than the water beneath, and it drifts as a shifting cover over the polar seas.

title: Drifting icebergs
text: An iceberg is a great mass of freshwater ice that has broken from a glacier or ice sheet and drifts out to sea. Most of its bulk lies hidden beneath the surface, which is why icebergs are so perilous to passing ships.

title: Waves and the shore
text: As waves reach the shore they shape the coast, wearing away headlands and building up beaches. Their ceaseless work moves sand along the shore and carves the cliffs, coves, and bars that give a coastline its form.

title: Longshore drift
text: Longshore drift is the slow movement of sand and shingle along a coast, driven by waves that strike the shore at an angle. Grain by grain it carries beach material one way, building spits and reshaping the shoreline over time.

title: Rip currents
text: A rip current is a narrow, strong flow of water rushing seaward from the shore, formed as water piled up by breaking waves finds a channel out. It can bear a swimmer swiftly away from land and is a hidden danger at many a beach.

title: Continental drift
text: Continental drift is the once-startling idea that the continents have slowly moved across the globe over vast ages. It is now understood as part of plate tectonics, in which great slabs of the Earth's crust drift upon the mantle below.

title: The abyss
text: The abyss is the deep, dark realm of the ocean far below the reach of sunlight. Cold, still, and immense, it was long thought barren, yet it teems with strange life adapted to its darkness, its cold, and its crushing pressure.

title: The ocean sound channel
text: Deep in the ocean lies a layer through which sound travels with least loss and can carry for thousands of kilometres. Sound waves bend back toward this channel, trapped within it, so that faint noises may be heard across whole ocean basins.

title: Tides and navigation
text: Sailors have long reckoned with the tides, timing their passage through shallow harbours and over bars to the rise and fall of the sea. Tables of the tides let them foresee when a channel will run deep enough to cross in safety.

title: Wind waves and swell
text: Near a storm the sea is a confused jumble of steep wind waves, but far away the same energy arrives as smooth, orderly swell. The long swell has outrun and outlasted the storm, sorting into rolling waves that reach distant shores.

title: Whitecaps on the sea
text: Whitecaps are the foaming crests that appear when the wind grows strong enough to blow the tops off the waves. Sailors read them as a sign of the wind's force, for they begin to form once the breeze reaches a certain steady strength.

title: The horizon at sea
text: Because the Earth is curved, one at sea can see only so far before the surface falls away below the horizon. The higher the eye, the farther the view, which is why lookouts climbed to the masthead to sight distant land or sails.

title: The curve of the sea
text: Though the sea looks flat to one standing on a ship, its surface follows the curve of the globe. Distant vessels sink hull-first below the horizon as they sail away, a plain token that the world is round.

title: Foam and bubbles
text: The white foam of breaking waves and the wake of ships is a froth of countless tiny air bubbles caught in the water. Trapped when air and water mix violently, the bubbles scatter light in all directions and so appear white.

title: The elements of the ancients
text: Long before modern chemistry, philosophers held that all things were made of a few elements, commonly earth, water, air, and fire. Though the notion was mistaken, it was an early attempt to reduce the world to a few basic substances.

title: Density and floating
text: Whether a thing floats or sinks depends on its density set against that of the water. A cork floats because it is lighter than an equal volume of water, while a stone sinks because it packs more matter into the same space.

title: Pressure and the deep
text: The deeper one goes beneath the sea, the greater the pressure, for the weight of all the water above bears down. At the greatest depths the pressure is immense, hundreds of times that at the surface, testing the strength of any vessel.

title: Sound and the ear
text: We hear when vibrations in the air, or in the water, reach the ear and set its delicate parts trembling. These small movements are turned into signals the mind reads as sound, from the faint lap of waves to the roar of the storm.

title: The compass and iron
text: A ship's iron and steel can disturb the compass, drawing the needle from true. Navigators learned to correct for this by setting balancing masses of iron nearby, so that the compass might once more point faithfully toward the pole.

title: Canals between seas
text: Great canals cut through narrow necks of land let ships pass between seas without the long voyage around whole continents. Such passages join oceans that nature kept apart, shortening the sea roads of the world.

title: Sea straits
text: A strait is a narrow channel of water joining two larger seas or oceans. Often busy with shipping and swept by strong currents, straits such as Gibraltar and Malacca have long been prized as gateways between the wider waters.

title: Gulfs and bays
text: A gulf or bay is a portion of the sea partly enclosed by land, curving inward from the coast. Sheltered from the open ocean, such waters have long offered harbours for ships and rich grounds for those who fish.

title: The equator and the sea
text: The equator circles the Earth midway between the poles, where the Sun stands highest and the sea is warmest. There the trade winds meet, driving the great equatorial currents that sweep warm water westward across the oceans.

title: The poles and the sea
text: At the cold poles the sea grows so chill that it freezes over, and its dense, cold water sinks to feed the deep currents of the world. These frozen ends of the Earth drive much of the slow circulation that stirs the whole ocean.

title: Coral islands
text: Coral islands rise where reef-building corals have grown up over ages upon a shallow foundation, building land above the sea. Low and ringed by reef, such islands support only the hardy plants and creatures able to endure salt and storm.

title: The lighthouse lens
text: The great lighthouses gather their light with a special lens of stepped rings that bends the beams into a single bright shaft. This clever lens, throwing a strong beam far out to sea from a modest flame, has warned ships from many a dangerous coast.

title: Waves refracting toward shore
text: As waves near the shore, the part in shallow water slows while the rest sweeps on, so the wave crest bends to follow the shape of the coast. This is why waves so often arrive nearly parallel to the beach, whatever their first direction.

title: The salinity of enclosed seas
text: In warm, enclosed seas where much water evaporates and little fresh flows in, the water grows saltier than the open ocean. Where cold rivers and rain pour into a sheltered sea, by contrast, its waters may be markedly less salt.

title: The sounding of the deep
text: To learn the depth of the deep sea, early surveyors lowered weighted lines thousands of fathoms to the bottom. It was slow and uncertain work, and only with such patient soundings did the true shape of the ocean floor begin to be known.

title: Ocean tides in narrow seas
text: In broad open oceans the tide rises and falls but modestly, yet where the water is funnelled into a narrowing gulf or channel it may pile up to a great height. The shape of the coast can thus turn a gentle ocean tide into a mighty one.
